2027–2030 budget request
business cases
How to read these business cases: The budget proposal description provides
the broader context and scope of the proposal, and may include elements
beyond what is funded in the proposed 2027–2030 Budget document. The
budget proposal description, benefits and risks sections should be read together
to understand the implications of the recommended funding level.

1 Accelerating Housing Development: Bill 20 and Residential Sub-
Classes
Budget proposal rationale: Explicit Direction from Council
Department: Corporate Planning & Financial Business unit: Assessment & Tax
Services
Budget proposal description
Council directed Administration to proceed with work to enable a Purpose-Built Rental Tax Exemption Program,
including further industry engagement and development of programs targeting Transit-Oriented Development
locations and high-rise rental housing in the Greater Downtown. This budget item responds to Council direction arising
from a Notice of Motion (EC2025-0117, EC2026-0018).
Proposed funding amount
2027 2028 2029 2030

Ongoing ($M) 0.1 - - -

=== page
2 Sustaining reliable CTrain rail infrastructure
Budget proposal rationale: Risk-based considerations
Department: Operational Services Business unit: Calgary Transit
Budget proposal description
This investment is required to maintain aging rail infrastructure, including signals, track, power systems, and crossing
gate arms. Without this funding, there is a risk to critical infrastructure failing, resulting in more frequent and longer
CTrain service disruptions for customers.

16 Facility Infrastructure
Department Business Unit
Calgary Police Services Calgary Police Services
Investment Description:
Calgary Police Services (CPS) manages a diverse portfolio of district offices, specialized operational buildings, training
centres, investigative facilities and administrative offices. Together, these spaces enable effective law enforcement and
community safety via safe, reliable and fit-to-purpose infrastructure. The portfolio consists of 41 buildings and their
associated parking lots, roads, sidewalks and grounds.
Nearly 40 per cent of the CPS' buildings are over 40 years old and will approach or surpass 50 years in 2031. Historic
underfunding has resulted in a significant backlog of deferred maintenance, and growing lifecycle and system risks,
requiring renewed investment.
Funding will address critical and urgent maintenance needs to keep buildings safe, functional and compliant, prioritizing
lifecycle optimization to prevent emergent replacement response, and allow for comprehensive space planning required for
an expanding policing workforce over the four-year planning and budget cycle.
This investment has been identified as Required.

17 Critical Infrastructure Annual Investment Program
Department Business Unit
Infrastructure Services Capital Planning & Business Services
Investment Description:
The City owns and operates critical infrastructure assets where failure could result in serious public safety risks, service
disruptions, and reputational impacts. Currently, the buildings portfolio encompasses over 100 critical facility assets, with
this count expected to grow as the asset management team continues building the Critical Asset Dashboard and refining
risk mitigation strategies.
Capital investment is required to proactively inspect, assess, and address safety‑critical risks across this portfolio. The
program primarily funds inspections, condition assessments, and interim stabilization measures to ensure critical assets or
their components do not pose an imminent risk to public safety while longer-term solutions are evaluated. Due to the
varied nature and condition of critical infrastructure issues, long-term repair and rehabilitation costs are often unknown at
the time of inspection and can vary significantly depending on the specific issue identified. Furthermore, significant data
gaps and unknowns remain regarding Community Association facilities. Ongoing condition and risk assessment work in
these community-managed assets is anticipated to uncover additional critical infrastructure requiring timely intervention.
This investment has been identified as Required.

18 Municipal Complex Upgrades
Department Business Unit
Operational Services Facilities
Investment Description:
This investment supports essential work and renovations to the Municipal Complex, including the Municipal Building,
Administrative Building, Historic City Hall, West Plaza and Civic Employee Memorial Garden. Several building systems are
reaching the end of their service life and require replacement to address safety, accessibility and legislative requirements.
Without this investment, The City faces increased risk of code non-compliance, constraints on future renovations, impacts to
occupancy permits and disruptions affecting more than 2,000 staff and elected officials. Funding will support compliance to
accessibility and fire-safety systems and replacement of aging chillers, stormwater piping, electrical feeders and building-
envelope components. The exterior plaza will also be improved to address accessibility needs and align with planned
improvements to Olympic Plaza and the Arts District. The Municipal Complex also supports in-person services such as Fair
Entry, transit pass sales, ENMAX payments and permit applications.

20 Shepard Snow Storage Site
Department Business Unit
Operational Services Mobility
Investment Description:
This infrastructure investment funds construction of the new Shepard Snow Storage site to replace the Highfield Snow
Storage facility, which must be decommissioned to accommodate the Green Line alignment. The loss of the Highfield
facility removes 55 per cent of the City's total snow storage capacity. Constructing the replacement site is an operational
necessity to maintain baseline winter service levels and prevent transportation network disruptions during major snowfall
events.

Primary Corporate Operating Risk: Community Relations Risk
How will this investment manage or mitigate the Primary Corporate Operating Risk?
This investment advances planning and design for an expanded and improved animal shelter. The future facility
improvements are intended to increase shelter capacity, provide appropriate space for animal care and adoption services,
and improve the functionality of spaces used by employees, animals and the public. Completing the planning and design
work will also establish project scope, requirements and cost information needed to inform future construction funding
decisions.
Risk(s) of Not Proceeding (Approving) This Capital Spending Request
Without this investment, the planning and design to address the Animal Services Centre's capacity and facility limitations
would not proceed. The existing Animal Services Centre will remain unable to meet growing demand for shelter, intake, and
adoption services, while continuing to operate from an aging facility that no longer supports modern animal welfare
standards or future growth requirements. Failure to invest will likely increase capacity constraints, resulting in more stray
and abandoned animals in the community, reduced ability to accept and care for animals in a timely manner, and missed
opportunities to improve adoption outcomes and associated revenues. The City will also face increasing community
relations and reputational risks as residents experience reduced service levels, limited access to animal services, and visible
impacts from unmanaged animal populations. Ultimately, not proceeding could erode public confidence in City services,
compromise animal welfare outcomes, and leave essential infrastructure deficiencies unresolved at a time when demand for
animal services continues to grow.
Risk(s) of Proceeding (Approving) This Capital Spending Request
The project faces execution risks related to scope development, cost estimates, schedule, procurement and coordination
with ongoing Animal Services operations. Planning and design may identify additional facility requirements or costs that
affect the scope and future funding required for construction. If future construction affects the existing facility, a temporary
operating strategy may also be required to maintain animal services during implementation. Because the current investment
does not include full construction funding, realization of the intended capacity and facility improvements will depend on
future capital decisions.

24 Hillsides Program – Slope Remediation
Department Business Unit
Infrastructure Services Public Spaces Delivery
Investment Description:
This geotechnical program expands structural stabilization and continuous monitoring of degraded hillsides across the
municipality. While existing funding limits Administration to preliminary assessments of poor slopes, proposed capital
stabilizes prioritized failing slopes that present public safety and infrastructure risks. The investment delivers engineering
investigations, detailed design, construction, and rehabilitation for priority locations, including Centre Street and 7th
Avenue, Douglas Fir Trail, Edworthy Park Access Road, Mount Alberta View, and other poorly performing slopes. Future
phases include the Klippert/Home Road Escarpment Slope Stability Project beyond the 2027 to 2030 cycle, alongside
additional sites identified through ongoing assessments to reduce geotechnical risks, improve asset resilience, and protect
adjacent public infrastructure from subsidence.

25 Retaining Wall Replacement Program
Department Business Unit
Infrastructure Services Public Spaces Delivery
Investment Description:
This annual capital program funds the replacement and structural rehabilitation of retaining walls across the city that are
assessed to be in fair, poor, or critical condition. Serving as foundational earth-retention structures, these assets are
required to stabilize slopes immediately adjacent to public roadways, active pathways, and municipal buildings. The current
investment prioritizes over 15 high-risk walls approaching the end of their engineering design life. By deploying modern
structural solutions, such as cast-in-place concrete and modular block systems, alongside comprehensive drainage and
erosion controls, the City secures the physical terrain. This intervention is necessary to prevent earth failures that would
sever mobility corridors.

26 Facilities Equipment & Technology (Water) Program
Department Business Unit
Infrastructure Services Utilities Delivery
Investment Description:
Facilities, Equipment & Technology Program delivers critical investments in digital systems, operational tools, laboratory
equipment, and facility upgrades required to support the safe, efficient delivery of water, wastewater, and stormwater
services. The program includes lifecycle replacement and enhancement of core technology platforms (e.g., asset and
workflow management systems), expansion of laboratory and regulatory assurance capabilities, and upgrades to
operational tools and equipment across drinking water, wastewater, and stormwater services. It also advances data
management and system integration (e.g., Maximo and OGIS), enabling improved asset visibility, decision-making, and
service efficiency. Collectively, these investments ensure regulatory compliance, modernize operations, and provide the
foundational systems and tools required to support reliable service delivery.
This investment has been identified as Required.
Investment Components:
Key investment components contributing to a significant portion of the 2027–2030 Budget Request for this program include
the following:
Equipment ($42M):
The City’s operational effectiveness is supported through ongoing investment in equipment, technology systems, and
specialized tools that enable reliable delivery of water services and regulatory compliance. This includes advancing AI and
emerging technologies, improving billing systems, maintaining and upgrading software and equipment lifecycles, and
strengthening asset data management platforms such as Maximo and OpenGIS. In addition, critical field and laboratory
equipment supporting drinking water distribution, wastewater and stormwater collection, repair and maintenance, and
water quality monitoring are being renewed and modernized. These assets are facing increasing pressure from aging
equipment, evolving regulatory requirements, growing service demands, and the need for more integrated and data-driven
operations. Investments in this category provide benefits through improved operational efficiency, enhanced data accuracy
and visibility, strengthened compliance with regulatory standards, and increased reliability of both field and laboratory
functions. Collectively, these initiatives mitigate key risks related to outdated or failing equipment, data gaps, inefficiencies
in maintenance and operations, and reduced ability to respond to system issues. Without these investments, the City would
face increased operational disruptions, reduced data integrity and decision-making capability, higher lifecycle and
maintenance costs, and greater risk of non-compliance with regulatory and service expectations.
Major projects within this component include Tools & Equipment ($20M), Billing Improvements ($6M), Software Upgrade
($10M), AI & Emerging Technology ($6M).
Building Upgrades ($15M):
The City’s facility infrastructure is supported through targeted building upgrades that enhance the functionality, safety, and
efficiency of critical operational spaces, including the Bearspaw Treatment Plant administrative areas, the Expansion and
Growth Operations Workplace Centre, and the Water Centre building. These assets are facing increasing pressure from
aging building systems, evolving workplace standards, and the need to accommodate a growing and more dynamic
workforce. Investments in these upgrades provide benefits through improved workspace efficiency, enhanced health and
safety conditions, and modernized building systems that support productivity and collaboration. They also enable better
alignment with current operational needs and future growth by optimizing space utilization and integrating updated
technologies. Collectively, these projects mitigate key risks related to deteriorating infrastructure, inefficient layouts, and
outdated systems that can hinder operations and staff effectiveness. Without these investments, the City would face
continued inefficiencies, increased maintenance and lifecycle costs, reduced staff productivity, and potential challenges in
supporting evolving operational and workforce requirements.

27 Stormwater Management Program
Department Business Unit
Infrastructure Services Utilities Delivery
Investment Description:
Drainage Facilities and Network supports the safe, reliable, and resilient management of stormwater for Calgarians. This
program maintains and enhances the infrastructure required to collect, convey, store, and manage stormwater across the
city, helping protect public safety, property, and critical infrastructure. The majority of investments within this program are
driven by the need to renew aging assets, support growth and development, manage flood risks, and maintain compliance
with regulatory and environmental requirements. Together, these investments help ensure Calgary's drainage system
remains resilient, sustainable, and capable of supporting a growing city both now and into the future.
This investment has been identified as Required.
Investment Components:
Key investment components contributing to a significant portion of the 2027–2030 Budget Request for this program include
the following:
Community Drainage Improvement Program ($135M):
The City’s Community Drainage Improvement Program supports safe and reliable stormwater management by upgrading
drainage infrastructure in established communities that are vulnerable to localized flooding. These assets are under
increasing pressure from aging or undersized infrastructure, more intense rainfall events, community growth, and evolving
stormwater and environmental requirements. Investments within this component improve drainage capacity, reduce flood
risk, protect public safety and property, and support environmental protection by improving how stormwater is collected,
conveyed, stored, and managed. Collectively, these investments help mitigate risks related to localized flooding, property
damage, unsafe conditions, service disruptions, and regulatory non-compliance.
Major projects within this component include Confederation Park ($36M), Northwest Inner City Hillhurst ($24M), Palliser
Oakridge ($17M), Northwest Inner City 14 Street Northwest ($14M), and the Local Drainage Improvements Annual
Investment Program ($4.5M).
Stormwater Lift Stations ($67M):
The City's stormwater lift stations support the reliable conveyance of stormwater in areas where gravity-based drainage
systems are not sufficient, helping protect communities, infrastructure, and receiving environments from flooding. These
assets are under increasing pressure from aging pumps, electrical systems, controls, and structural components, as well as
increasing rainfall intensity and evolving regulatory requirements. Investments within this component renew and upgrade
critical lift station infrastructure to maintain reliable system performance, reduce flood risk, and support regulatory
compliance. Collectively, these investments help mitigate risks associated with equipment failures, uncontrolled stormwater
discharge, environmental impacts, and service disruptions. Without these investments, the City would face increased risk of
flooding, regulatory non-compliance, environmental impacts, and costly emergency repairs.
Major projects within this component include the 9th Avenue Downtown Underpass Stormwater Lift Station ($50M) and the
Stormwater Lift Station Annual Investment Program ($12M).
Stormwater Trunks ($61M):
The City's stormwater trunk infrastructure provides the major conveyance capacity required to collect and transport
stormwater runoff from developing and established areas to downstream drainage systems and receiving waters. These
investments are critical to supporting growth by ensuring sufficient drainage capacity is available to accommodate new
communities, employment areas, and future development. Investments within this component expand and enhance the
stormwater network, helping manage flood risks, maintain service levels, and support long-term city growth. Without these
ISC: UNRESTRICTED 2027–2030 Budget: Investing for the future 62

=== page
investments, growth opportunities may be constrained, drainage capacity shortfalls could emerge, and the City would face
increased risks associated with flooding, servicing limitations, and delayed development.
Major projects within this component include the Prairie Economic Gateway Storm Trunk to Shepard Ditch ($39M),
Providence Storm Trunk Stages 3 & 4 ($20M), and the Saatoohtsi Storm Trunk and Outfall ($2M).
Storm Pond Repairs and Upgrades ($29M):
The City's storm ponds play a critical role in managing stormwater runoff, reducing flood risk, improving water quality, and
protecting downstream waterways. Investments within this component are primarily focused on maintaining and
rehabilitating existing stormwater assets, including pond structures, embankments, erosion controls, sediment management
systems, and safety features. As these assets age, ongoing maintenance and renewal are required to preserve storage
capacity, environmental performance, and regulatory compliance. Collectively, these investments help mitigate risks
associated with flooding, erosion, sediment accumulation, deteriorating infrastructure, and environmental impacts.
Major projects within this component include the Storm Pond Sediment Management Project ($10M), the Pond Renewal
Annual Investment Program ($7M), and the Storm Pond Safety Annual Investment Program ($5M).
Dam Safety Management ($18M):
The City’s dam safety infrastructure supports the safe and reliable operation of stormwater management facilities by
maintaining dam structures, monitoring systems, and associated safety controls. These assets play a critical role in
protecting downstream communities, infrastructure, and the environment from flooding and uncontrolled releases.
Investments within this component help maintain compliance with provincial dam safety regulations, reduce the risk of
structural deterioration or failure, and support the long-term resiliency of stormwater infrastructure. Several assets within
this component have been identified as having a Severe Consequence of Failure within The City's 2026 Corporate Asset
Management Plan, highlighting the significant public safety, environmental, and service impacts that could result from asset
failure. Without these investments, the City would face increased risk of regulatory non-compliance, infrastructure failure,
downstream flooding, and significant safety and environmental consequences.
Major projects within this component include a New Pond Dam Safety Project ($8M), Discovery Ridge Dam Removal and
Landscape Design ($6M), and the Stormwater Management Facility Dam Safety Program Annual Investment Program ($4M).

Primary Corporate Operating Risk: Growth Risk
How will this investment manage or mitigate the Primary Corporate Operating Risk?
This program addresses Growth Risk by ensuring landfill and treatment infrastructure capacity keeps pace with Calgary's
increasing population and economic growth. Continued growth places pressure on landfill cells, treatment facilities, and
supporting infrastructure, creating the risk of capacity constraints and asset deterioration if investments are deferred.
Investments in , cell construction, landfill maintenance, capping, remediation, and long-term planning help ensure The City

Risk(s) of Not Proceeding (Approving) This Capital Spending Request

failures that could disrupt waste disposal services city‑wide. Deferred action increases the likelihood of regulatory
non‑compliance, environmental harm, and emergency interventions that are far more costly and damaging to public trust.
Risk(s) of Proceeding (Approving) This Capital Spending Request

infrastructure while maintaining uninterrupted essential services. The work is highly dependent on factors outside of the
Service’s direct control, including contractor availability, regulatory approvals, and constrained construction windows tied to
operational requirements. These risks are mitigated through phased implementation, conservative scheduling and formal
project management and governance measures embedded through the Capital Planning Process.

30 Wastewater Collection Network Program
Department Business Unit
Infrastructure Services Utilities Delivery
Investment Description:
Wastewater Collection Network program delivers integrated investments across trunk sewers, lift stations, siphons, and local
collection infrastructure to maintain reliable service in existing communities, enable growth in developing areas, and
address state‑of‑good‑repair needs. The program includes major trunk expansions and upgrades such as Nose Creek,
Shepard, Providence, and Prairie Economic Gateway servicing, alongside extensive renewal work including sewer upgrades,
trenchless rehabilitation, and replacement programs targeting aging and critical infrastructure. It also advances system
reliability and performance through lift station replacements, cathodic protection, condition assessments, and control
system upgrades. Collectively, these investments strengthen system capacity, reduce failure risks, and improve the overall
resilience and functionality of the wastewater collection network.
This investment has been identified as Required.
Investment Components:
Key investment components contributing to a significant portion of the 2027–2030 Budget Request for this program include
the following:
Sanitary Network - Linear Assets ($292M):
The City’s wastewater collection system is sustained through ongoing rehabilitation, replacement, and expansion of critical
sanitary linear infrastructure, including trunk sewers, local mains, service connections, and supporting network components
across established and growth areas. This program includes targeted replacements of high-risk assets, condition
assessments, redevelopment initiatives, and major trunk upgrades to support system capacity and long-term reliability.
These assets are facing increasing pressure from aging pipes, urban growth, increased hydraulic demand, and the need to
maintain performance in densely developed and environmentally sensitive areas. Investments in this category provide
benefits through improved system capacity, enhanced reliability, reduced risk of overflows, and more effective asset
management and lifecycle planning. Collectively, these initiatives mitigate key risks related to pipe failures, sewer backups,
capacity constraints, and environmental contamination from overflows or leaks. Without these investments, the City would
face increased service disruptions, higher frequency of emergency repairs, reduced system performance, and escalating
impacts to public health, the environment, and operating costs. An additional $94.4M has been pre-approved for this work

resilience across the network. This includes upgrades and replacements of lift stations, ongoing capital maintenance,
condition assessments, and enhancements to electrical and control systems, as well as cathodic protection and siphon
infrastructure improvements. These assets are under increasing pressure from aging equipment, rising service demand, and
the need to maintain reliable performance in both established and growth areas. Investments in this category provide
benefits through improved system reliability, enhanced operational control, increased resilience to equipment or power
failures, and extended asset life. Collectively, these initiatives mitigate key risks related to pump failures, conveyance
disruptions, corrosion, and reduced system redundancy. Without these investments, the City would face increased risk of

32 Water Distribution Network Program
Department Business Unit
Infrastructure Services Utilities Delivery
Investment Description:
Water Distribution Network program delivers integrated investments across transmission mains, pump stations, reservoirs,
metering infrastructure, and control systems to maintain reliable service in existing communities and enable growth in new
development areas. The program includes major city-shaping infrastructure such as North and South Water Servicing
strategies, Providence/Starlight growth infrastructure, and key feedermain expansions, alongside extensive state-of-good-
repair work including main and valve replacements, cathodic protection, and rehabilitation. It also advances system
optimization through advanced metering infrastructure, district metering, leak detection, and control system upgrades.
Collectively, these investments strengthen network capacity, reliability, and operational visibility to support safe, efficient
delivery of potable water across the city.
This investment has been identified as Required.
Investment Components:
Key investment components contributing to a significant portion of the 2027–2030 Budget Request for this program include
the following:
Water Servicing ($254M):
The City’s water servicing system sustains reliable and efficient delivery of potable water by advancing critical feedermains
and energy recovery infrastructure to manage system pressures, support distribution capacity, and optimize operational
performance across the network. This system is facing significant pressure from continued urban growth, increasing demand
in developing areas (particularly North Calgary), and the need to balance pressure management with system efficiency and
asset longevity. These investments provide benefits through improved reliability, enhanced pressure management,
increased energy recovery, and reduced water loss by minimizing system stress, lowering the likelihood of leaks and failures,
and supporting more efficient system operation. Collectively, they mitigate key risks related to inadequate or aging servicing
infrastructure that could lead to pressure-related failures, service disruptions, increased non-revenue water, and higher
operating costs. Without these investments, the City would face reduced system resilience, greater risk of asset failure and
water loss, and escalating operational and emergency response costs. An additional $368.3M has been pre-approved for
work on the North Calgary Water Servicing Facility in 2027-2030.
Major projects within this component include South Calgary Water Servicing Feedermain ($243M), North and South Calgary
Energy Recovery Stations ($10.6M).
Feedermains & Mains ($398M):
The City’s transmission and distribution network sustains reliable delivery of safe drinking water by renewing and upgrading
critical water mains and feedermains to address asset lifecycle needs, maintain system capacity, and improve overall
reliability and redundancy across the network. The system is facing increasing pressure from aging infrastructure, meeting
service expectations, urban growth, and the criticality of large-diameter feedermains where failures have high consequence
impacts. These investments provide benefits through improved service continuity, reduced water loss, enhanced fire
protection, and strengthened system resilience, while mitigating key risks related to asset failure, large-scale service
outages, water quality impacts, and safety risks to the public and operators. Without these investments, the City would face
increasing main breaks, potential catastrophic feedermain failures, reduced network performance, and escalating emergency
repair and maintenance costs. An additional $21.1M has been pre-approved for this work in 2027-2030.
Major projects within this component include Main & Feedermain Replacements and Extenstions ($206.4M), Feedermains:
Prairie Economic Gateway ($62M), Country Hills Boulevard Crosstie ($39M), Providence Westview ($26M), Starlight ($25M),
Westview Crestmont ($16M).

control across the distribution network. These assets are experiencing growing pressure from aging condition, increased
demand variability, and higher expectations for system responsiveness and redundancy during outages or emergencies.
These investments provide benefits through improved service continuity, enhanced fire protection, strengthened system
resilience, and reduced water loss by improving isolation capability, minimizing leak duration, and supporting more efficient
system operation. Collectively, they mitigate key risks related to asset failure, pressure loss, limited system control, and

timely access for maintenance and repairs. Collectively, these initiatives mitigate key risks related to asset degradation,
undetected leaks, equipment failure, and limited system visibility that could lead to service disruptions, increased non-

reduced ability to detect and respond to leaks, accelerated infrastructure deterioration, and higher long-term operating and

Primary Corporate Operating Risk: Asset Risk
How will this investment manage or mitigate the Primary Corporate Operating Risk?
This investment reduces operational and asset risk by by renewing and maintaining critical building assets before failure
occurs, helping ensure municipal facilities remain safe, reliable, and available to support service delivery. The program
reduces the risk of unplanned outages, service disruptions, health and safety incidents, and escalating maintenance costs by
addressing aging infrastructure in a proactive and systematic manner. Sustaining facility assets also extends asset life,
preserves service levels, supports regulatory compliance, and protects the City's investment in its building portfolio.
Risk(s) of Not Proceeding (Approving) This Capital Spending Request
Without this investment, the facility maintenance backlog will increase as assets continue to age and deteriorate. This will
increase the likelihood of service disruptions, facility outages and unplanned repairs, placing greater pressure on
maintenance resources and operating costs. Over time, facility reliability may decline, health and safety risks will increase,
and more extensive rehabilitation or replacement will be required.
Risk(s) of Proceeding (Approving) This Capital Spending Request
Communities expect City assets, facilities and parks to be safe, reliable and well maintained. Over the past four years, age-
and condition-based maintenance needs have outpaced available funding. At the recommended funding level, The City is
not expected to achieve its target of limiting facilities in Poor or Very Poor condition to 12 percent, with approximately 13.3
percent forecast to be in these condition categories by 2030. As assets continue to age and deteriorate, outstanding
maintenance needs will remain, increasing the potential for more extensive rehabilitation or replacement, higher future
costs, service disruptions, and assets becoming unsafe or unavailable for use. Market conditions, funding availability and
competing priorities may also affect project scope, schedules and costs, with some work potentially extending over multiple
years. The City will continue to prioritize maintenance and renewal needs to manage the highest risks; however,
outstanding asset-condition and project execution risks will remain at the recommended funding level.

How will this investment manage or mitigate the Primary Corporate Operating Risk?
This program replaces aging street lighting infrastructure to maintain compliance with modern electrical standards,
mitigating electrical safety hazards and outages caused by poles exceeding their 50-year design life. Targeted renewals of
degraded poles, conduits, and relays meet Canadian Electrical Code requirements, securing nighttime visibility for all road
users and preventing systemic illumination failures.
Risk(s) of Not Proceeding (Approving) This Capital Spending Request
Increases the risk of fallen poles and associated public safety hazards, contributes to public perception of deteriorating
infrastructure, and could lead to neighbourhood blackouts and lower citizen satisfaction.
Risk(s) of Proceeding (Approving) This Capital Spending Request
The network includes approximately 18,000 poles exceeding their 50-year design life, requiring systematic lifecycle
management to address electrical and structural conditions along public rights-of-way. To manage aging infrastructure, the
program prioritizes assets through condition-based field inspections. The recommended funding level supports ongoing
condition inspections and approximately 7 scheduled pole replacements annually, while full capital funding in line with
2027-2030 needs accelerates delivery to systematically address the degrading asset backlog. During 2026, 5 pole
replacements occurred out of the 17,000 poles identified in Sub-Optimal operating condition (representing 17 per cent of
the system). Under the recommended funding level, this asset backlog increases from 17 per cent to 21 per cent of the
system, projecting approximately 7 pole replacements per year. Reactive repairs incur higher unit costs than scheduled
lifecycle replacements, while increasing localized outages and maintenance demands along high-traffic corridors. Fully
funding 2027 to 2030 capital needs systematically upgrades the network to Canadian Electrical Code standards,
modernizing to LED luminaires to enhance nighttime visibility, reduce energy consumption, and lower municipal emissions.

Primary Corporate Operating Risk: Asset Risk
How will this investment manage or mitigate the Primary Corporate Operating Risk?
This lifecycle program repairs and renews Calgary's road network to meet Level of Service targets. Delaying preventative
maintenance accelerates network deterioration, leading to expensive full-depth reconstructions. Sustained annual
investment protects the subgrade and renews pavement across arterial and community routes, optimizing asset lifespans
and maintaining the structural integrity of the roadway.
Risk(s) of Not Proceeding (Approving) This Capital Spending Request
Not proceeding increases asset deterioration, increases lifecycle costs, and reduces the ability to meet pavement condition
targets, ultimately requiring more expensive full-depth road reconstructions over time.
Risk(s) of Proceeding (Approving) This Capital Spending Request
Deferring pavement rehabilitation expands the backlog of roads requiring full reconstruction due to subgrade deterioration.
Road reconstruction costs 7 to 10 times more than pavement rehabilitation while delivering the same infrastructure life
extension, creating longer community disruptions, poorer ride quality, freight impediments, and higher future liabilities. The
current road network condition is 34 per cent good, 42 per cent fair, and 24 per cent poor, against a 10-year Council-
approved Level of Service target of 50 per cent good, 27 per cent fair, and 23 per cent poor. Funding the program as
outlined in the 10-year Capital Infrastructure Plan improves conditions to 37 per cent good, 42 per cent fair, and 21 per cent
poor by 2030. Under the proposed funding level, the network reaches 32 per cent good, 44 per cent fair, and 24 per cent
poor by 2030, with 2 per cent of good roads degrading to fair while delivering 2,547 lane-km of repaving compared to
3,300 lane-km if fully funded.

63 Vehicle & Equipment Replacement
Department Business Unit
Operational Services Fleet & Inventory
Investment Description:
This lifecycle investment replaces vehicles and equipment necessary to sustain existing Council-approved services. As
Calgary grows, fleet assets remain foundational to constructing, operating, inspecting, and maintaining City infrastructure.
Without reliable fleet availability, service delivery capacity declines and the intended benefits of many other City
investments cannot be fully realized.
Fleet & Inventory replaces vehicles and equipment on a continuous, planned basis rather than replacing large portions of
the fleet at periodic intervals. Maintaining a consistent annual replacement volume provides local vendors with predictable,
sustainable revenue, allowing both The City and its suppliers to deliver the program effectively. Without this approach,
replacement needs would accumulate into major procurement cycles, requiring approximately 2,000 units every four to five
years which is not practical.
Following post-COVID supply chain constraints, one-third of The City’s vehicle and equipment assets are now in “Very Poor”
condition and operating beyond their planned service life. This budget addresses these assets, along with those nearing the
end of their lifecycle. As assets age, maintenance costs and downtime increase, placing greater pressure on operating
budgets and increasing safety risks for City employees and the public. As an example, an excavator for Water Services
operating one year past its planned lifecycle saw maintenance costs increase from an average of $12,913/year to $32,456 in
the final year of operation. This cost does not include the associated downtime and associated mitigation measures
required to meet demand for the job function.

Benefits:
This investment supports responsible and sustainable lifecycle management of The City's vehicles and equipment by
replacing assets at the appropriate point in their lifecycle. Timely replacement helps control maintenance and operating
costs, reduce unplanned downtime, improve fleet availability, and avoid the escalating costs and risks associated with
operating assets beyond their intended service life.
Reliable and available vehicles and equipment are essential to delivering Council-approved services across the city.
Maintaining fleet capacity supports winter maintenance, emergency infrastructure repairs, waste collection, road and
pathway maintenance, and other frontline operations that Calgarians rely upon every day. Replacement assets improves
safety, regulatory compliance, operational efficiency, and environmental performance through newer technologies,
enhanced safety features, and improved fuel efficiency.
Primary Corporate Operating Risk: Operational Risk
How will this investment manage or mitigate the Primary Corporate Operating Risk?
This investment mitigates operational risk by supporting responsible and sustainable lifecycle management of The City's
vehicles and equipment. Replacing assets at the appropriate point in their lifecycle helps maintain the fleet capacity
required to deliver existing Council-approved service levels while reducing the risk of breakdowns, unplanned downtime,
service disruptions, and escalating maintenance costs.
Older on-road vehicles become increasingly difficult and costly to maintain in compliance with provincial commercial
carrier, regulatory, and safety requirements. Timely replacement helps maintain vehicle roadworthiness, supports continued
compliance with operating requirements, and reduces the risk of service interruptions caused by extended maintenance
activities or vehicle availability constraints.
The investment also helps prevent replacement needs from accumulating into larger future procurement cycles that would
be more costly, operationally challenging, and difficult for suppliers and City resources to support. Maintaining a consistent
replacement program improves fleet availability, strengthens operational readiness, and supports the safe, reliable, and
cost-effective delivery of frontline services relied upon by Calgarians.
Risk(s) of Not Proceeding (Approving) This Capital Spending Request
Failure to replace vehicles and equipment at the appropriate point in their lifecycle because of insufficient budget or
deferral to future years would increase operational risk and place growing pressure on operating budgets. As assets age
beyond their planned service life, maintenance requirements, emergency repairs, downtime, rental costs and outsourced
services increase, transferring costs from the capital program to the operating budget while providing lower asset
availability and reliability.
Fleet maintenance capacity is already under increasing pressure. Continuing to operate growing numbers of aging assets
would require more maintenance resources, shop capacity, parts, and external vendor support at a time when vendor
availability is becoming increasingly constrained. Older on-road vehicles also become more difficult and costly to maintain
in compliance with commercial carrier safety and regulatory requirements, increasing inspection, repair, and corrective
maintenance demands. As maintenance needs exceed available capacity, asset downtime and service interruptions are likely
to increase.
Reduced fleet availability would affect the delivery of Council-approved services including winter maintenance, waste
collection, emergency infrastructure repairs, road and pathway maintenance, and other frontline operations. The impact may
also extend to other City capital investments that rely on vehicles and equipment to construct, operate, inspect, maintain, or
support new infrastructure and services.
Risk(s) of Proceeding (Approving) This Capital Spending Request
Proceeding may create budget pressure from market volatility. Careful planning will be required to ensure maintenance,
fueling or charging infrastructure, and vendor support are in place to minimize service impacts.

Risk(s) of Not Proceeding (Approving) This Capital Spending Request
Tenant health and safety risks increase as building systems age without planned lifecycle work, creating potential hazards,
service disruptions that may include potential unit closures and emergency relocations, and reputational risk to The City.
Deferring lifecycle work also increases the final costs of required maintenance work. If we do not preserve the existing non-
market housing stock, the benefits of housing supply growth from new units will be negated.
Risk(s) of Proceeding (Approving) This Capital Spending Request
Approving this investment commits The City to ongoing lifecycle reinvestment in Calgary Housing-owned assets and may
create expectations for continued municipal funding support for housing infrastructure. However, the proposed funding
levels align with the approved 10-year capital infrastructure plan and asset management strategy, mitigating the risk of
unplanned financial pressures. The investment supports proactive asset stewardship, reduces the likelihood of costly
emergency repairs and service disruptions, and helps maintain safe, reliable housing assets in a state of good repair.

to Calgary’s transportation network and require coordinated, long-term planning to remain reliable, safe, and cost-effective

decisions may become more reactive, increasing lifecycle costs and the risk of declining asset performance.
This investment will enable the City to identify emerging needs earlier, prioritize investments based on risk and lifecycle
considerations, and coordinate capital and operating decisions more effectively. In the ideal state, major mobility assets are
managed proactively to extend their service life, improve reliability, reduce long-term costs, and support a sustainable
transportation network.

Capital investment is required to renew the specialized operational facilities, shop equipment and supporting infrastructure

Calgarians.
Demand for Fleet & Inventory services has grown significantly as operational responsibilities have, and City service demands
continue to increase. Existing operational facilities and equipment are operating at or near capacity, while aging cranes,
ventilation systems, maintenance-support equipment, work areas and related infrastructure are becoming increasingly
difficult and costly to maintain. These constraints reduce operational efficiency, create workflow bottlenecks, increase
operational risk, and limit Fleet & Inventory's ability to meet current and future service demands.
This investment renews critical operational infrastructure within and around the facilities, replaces aging shop equipment,
addresses safety and compliance requirements, and improves the capacity and efficiency of Fleet & Inventory operations. By
strengthening the infrastructure required to maintain and support City assets, Fleet & Inventory can reduce maintenance
delays, improve turnaround times, increase asset availability and continue providing reliable support to the City services that
residents depend upon.

73 Natural Infrastructure Investments to reduce physical climate and
environmental risk
Department Business Unit
Planning & Development Services Environmental Risk & Resilience
Investment Description:
This initiative protects existing natural assets and integrates Natural Infrastructure (NI) into City planning, asset
management and capital delivery. The program includes updated data, financial valuation tools, funding for NI projects in
priority communities and grows the Conservation Reserve Fund for land acquisition and ecological restoration. Investing in
NI projects is important to shift from high-cost grey infrastructure (pipes and concrete) to nature-based solutions, like
wetlands, forests and grasslands, that offer multiple services and can provide a higher return on investment. By valuing
natural assets as core municipal infrastructure, the City can reduce long-term maintenance costs, enhance community
resilience, and meet rising climate adaptation demands more affordably.

Primary Corporate Operating Risk: Climate Risk
How will this investment manage or mitigate the Primary Corporate Operating Risk?
This investment treats natural assets (wetlands, forests, grasslands) as critical infrastructure that provides $2.5B in annual
service value. It mitigates risk by utilizing "nature-based solutions" for flood mitigation and heat reduction, which are often
more resilient than traditional grey infrastructure. Formalizing a Conservation Reserve ensures the City maintains the
ecosystem services necessary to protect communities from extreme weather events, reducing long-term disaster recovery
costs.
Risk(s) of Not Proceeding (Approving) This Capital Spending Request
Climate impacts are projected to rise to ~$2.6B/year by the 2050s, increasing pressure on municipal infrastructure and
budgets. Not investing increases reliance on higher-cost grey infrastructure solutions and limits the multi-functional
benefits of natural areas; heightens risk of environmental degradation and loss of ecosystem services; reduces capacity to
manage flooding, urban heat, and climate impacts; and results in higher long-term costs and reduced resilience.
Risk(s) of Proceeding (Approving) This Capital Spending Request
At the proposed funding level, the Conservation Reserve Fund would not receive funding in this business cycle. This will limit
The City's ability to protect natural areas at risk from development, strengthen ecosystem connections, restore ecological
assets, and secure external funding that could further support conservation and restoration initiatives. At the proposed
funding level, the program advances the City’s Natural Asset Valuation Program and provides funding for natural
infrastructure projects in priority communities. Risks of proceeding include the potential for nature-based solutions not
delivering benefits within the same timeframe as traditional infrastructure and their performance, under extreme climate
conditions, can be uncertain. Additional risks include challenges related to land acquisition and stakeholder coordination, as
well as the need for long-term stewardship and maintenance commitments to achieve intended outcomes.

74 Fleet Fuel Diversification Program
Department Business Unit
Operational Services Fleet & Inventory
Investment Description:
This investment strengthens The City's long-term fuel security and operational resilience by preparing today for the future
fueling needs of City services. Funding will support the infrastructure, systems, testing, and operational readiness required
to diversify the energy sources used by The City's fleet and equipment, including electric, hydrogen, and other alternative
fuel technologies.
Reliable access to fuel and energy is essential to maintaining fleet availability and supporting the Transit, emergency
response, utility, and municipal services that Calgarians depend on. Reliance on a single fuel source increases exposure to
future fuel supply disruptions, market volatility, infrastructure constraints, and evolving vehicle technologies.
This investment reduces that risk by establishing the infrastructure and organizational capability needed to support multiple
fuel and energy sources. By improving fuel security, operational flexibility, and long-term preparedness, The City will be
better positioned to maintain reliable service delivery, adapt to changing energy markets, and support future fleet
requirements as service demands continue to grow.

Primary Corporate Operating Risk: Asset Risk
How will this investment manage or mitigate the Primary Corporate Operating Risk?
Investment addresses corporate asset risk associated with deferred maintenance and deterioration of aging assets through
planned lifecycle maintenance based on completed Building Condition Assessments and Asset Management Plans. Current
investment will maintain existing asset conditions or mitigate rate of accumulated deferred maintenance. Addressing
deferred maintenance extends the life of the facilities and mitigates long-term operating costs due to aging infrastructure.
Planned maintenance mitigates the risk of unplanned shutdowns that impact public safety and quality of service.
Risk(s) of Not Proceeding (Approving) This Capital Spending Request
More capital needs would remain unaddressed, increasing the likelihood of asset deterioration, service disruptions and
more significant future interventions. Lack of long-term investment will result in potential safety risks, increase the likelihood
of unplanned shutdowns, potential asset failure or asset surrender and potential damage to The City’s reputation.
Risk(s) of Proceeding (Approving) This Capital Spending Request
Funding timing may affect Civic Partners’ ability to plan and complete maintenance. Current investment level will maintain
existing asset conditions or slow rate of deterioration of existing Partner facilities by addressing priority maintenance. The
City actively manages these risks with Civic Partners to minimize the likelihood of this risk.

81 Ditch Reconstruction
Department Business Unit
Operational Services Mobility
Investment Description:
This investment maintains the municipal network of roadside ditches to ensure effective surface drainage and preserve the
structural integrity of paved assets. Proper water management aligns with the need to protect road base layers from
subgrade saturation. Prioritizing these interventions stabilizes corridors and mitigates future liability associated with
flooding. Residents benefit from consistent roadway performance and a reduced need for emergency pavement repairs.

Primary Corporate Operating Risk: Asset Risk
How will this investment manage or mitigate the Primary Corporate Operating Risk?
Systematic reconstruction of roadside ditches to ensure effective surface drainage. The primary risk is the physical damage
to road base layers caused by subgrade saturation and freeze-thaw cycles. Proper water management is required to
preserve the structural integrity of paved assets. Prioritizing these interventions allows the City to stabilize vulnerable
corridors, protecting foundational roadway investments and reducing the need for emergency pavement repairs.
Risk(s) of Not Proceeding (Approving) This Capital Spending Request
Ditches continue to deteriorate, causing surface water pooling, road subgrade saturation, accelerated pavement failure, and
potential flooding damage to adjacent properties.
Risk(s) of Proceeding (Approving) This Capital Spending Request
The primary risk involves managing subgrade saturation and freeze-thaw impacts on road base layers resulting from surface
drainage conditions. Delivery considerations include construction staging and variability in subsurface conditions that may
affect drainage performance and restoration costs. The proposed level of funding moderates the delivery pace for
reconstruction and maintenance across the municipal roadside ditch network. This extends subgrade moisture exposure
along select paved assets, increasing the potential for accelerated pavement wear and requiring ongoing operating
maintenance to manage surface pooling, erosion, and localized drainage conditions. Deferring comprehensive ditch
restoration requires continued monitoring to manage localized flooding and maintain corridor performance. Fully funding
this investment to 2027-2030 needs stabilizes priority drainage corridors, protecting foundational roadway investments and
deferring full-depth reconstructions. Effective surface water management controls runoff, mitigates erosion, and protects
adjacent natural systems while supporting consistent network reliability.

82 GamePLAN - Wave 1 Projects
Department Business Unit
Community Services Recreation & Social Programs
Investment Description:
GamePLAN Wave 1 advances the first phase of The City’s 25-year strategy for public recreation. Calgary’s recreation system
is under pressure from aging facilities, population growth and increasing demand, creating risks to facility reliability, service
capacity and access to recreation. Wave 1 focuses on system stabilization by renewing aging infrastructure, addressing
priority service gaps and expanding capacity. The program includes 17 prioritized projects at different stages of readiness.
The recommended investment will advance priority projects through planning, design and construction based on system
need, facility condition, project readiness and available funding. This approach enables The City to direct capital to the
highest-priority recreation needs while progressing toward the service levels established through GamePLAN. Advocacy is
ongoing with other levels of government to secure additional funding which will allow more projects to proceed.

Primary Corporate Operating Risk: Asset Risk
How will this investment manage or mitigate the Primary Corporate Operating Risk?
GamePLAN Wave 1 mitigates risks to recreation service continuity and infrastructure reliability by directing investment to
priority facility renewal and capacity needs. Renewing aging facilities reduces the likelihood that deteriorating infrastructure
results in service disruption, facility closure or loss of recreation capacity. Investments in new and expanded capacity
respond to service gaps and increasing demand as Calgary grows. The system-wide prioritization approach directs available
funding to identified needs based on factors such as facility condition, service need and project readiness, reducing risk
across the recreation system while recognizing that some infrastructure and capacity needs will remain beyond the 2027–
2030 investment period.
Risk(s) of Not Proceeding (Approving) This Capital Spending Request
Without this investment, priority GamePLAN projects would not advance as planned, reducing The City’s ability to address
aging recreation infrastructure and identified service-capacity gaps. Facility condition would continue to deteriorate,
increasing the likelihood of service disruptions, closures and loss of recreation capacity. Capacity additions and facility
improvements needed to respond to population growth and demand would also occur later or require future funding
decisions.
Risk(s) of Proceeding (Approving) This Capital Spending Request
The recommended funding level advances GamePLAN Wave 1 but does not complete all identified Wave 1 projects.
Projects will therefore need to be sequenced according to priority, readiness and available funding. Recreation infrastructure
and service-capacity risks will remain for projects that do not advance within the 2027–2030 period, and additional
investment will be required to continue Wave 1 implementation. Individual projects also remain subject to changes in scope,
cost and schedule as planning, design and procurement progress.

reputational risk to the municipality if noise levels continuously exceed the 65-decibel transportation policy threshold. The
investment aims to address up to 10 walls on The City’s backlog list based on current funding projections. New potential
barrier locations are annually being measured based on current citizen complaints. This proram is being continuously
updated with priority locations.

Primary Corporate Operating Risk: Operational Risk
How will this investment manage or mitigate the Primary Corporate Operating Risk?
The existing asphalt plant requires lifecycle renewal as it operates nine years beyond its design service life, presenting the
risk of a total loss of year-round internal asphalt production capacity. Funding the full lifecycle replacement protects winter
road repairs following watermain breaks, supports spring pothole patching, and stabilizes pavement rehabilitation levels of
service. The replacement increases production capacity by over 200 per cent and incorporates reclaimed asphalt pavement
(RAP) capabilities to divert landfill waste, ensuring material supply continuity and cost efficiency for municipal maintenance.
Risk(s) of Not Proceeding (Approving) This Capital Spending Request
The Manchester Asphalt Plant is 44 years old and nine years beyond its intended service life, experiencing component
failures and production delays from reactive repairs. Not proceeding results in the total loss of year-round internal asphalt
production capacity, lost revenue potential, and heightened exposure to private market pricing and availability. This directly
impairs the ability to perform winter repairs following watermain breaks, citywide spring pothole patching, and scheduled
pavement rehabilitation, as private commercial plants do not operate during winter or early spring. Relying entirely on
external asphalt suppliers foregoes $5.6 million in annual operating efficiencies and up to $12 million in combined savings
and net revenue potential, while exposing capital programs to commercial pricing surges and supply chain delays.
Risk(s) of Proceeding (Approving) This Capital Spending Request
Replacing the Manchester Asphalt Plant ensures reliable production of year-round hot mix asphalt to restore roads in winter
and complete repairs in spring and summer. A modern automated facility reduces operating costs and expands production
capacity by more than 200 per cent. New equipment enables the production of sustainable mixes using reclaimed asphalt
pavement (RAP), meeting market demand for lower-cost mixes while diverting material from landfills. Improved production
capacity and operational efficiency generate an estimated net revenue potential of approximately $6.4 million, which can be
reinvested into roadway rehabilitation to improve network condition and service levels.

TO ITY OUNCIL
FROM THE CALGARY POLICE COMMISSION
PROPOSED 2027-2030 POLICE BUSINESS PLAN AND BUDGET
DATE: JULY 13, 2026
PURPOSE: ☒FOR INFORMATION ☐OTHER:
APPROVED BY: AMTUL SIDDIQUI, COMMISSION CHAIR
REASON FOR THIS MEMORANDUM
This memorandum provides additional information on the rationale and return on
investment for the proposed 2027-2030 police budget. A more detailed presentation
and information package will be provided to Council as part of the fall budget process.
DISCUSSION
The 2027-2030 police business plan and budget will be a forward-looking investment in
public safety, community trust and operational excellence. It is a forward-looking
budget that centres on providing more patrol officers to the frontline and ensuring they
have the tools, infrastructure and support to do their jobs efficiently and effectively.
Foundation for Budget Proposal
The Calgary Police Service (CPS) budget has not kept pace with Calgary’s population
growth and the increasing complexity of policing. Year after year, the CPS has absorbed
the increased workload through efficiencies and employee overtime. However, the
unsustainability of this approach is now showing through noticeably reduced service
levels, decreased employee retention, and employees on leave and accommodation.
i
ISC: UNRESTRICTED 2027–2030 Budget: Investing for the future 226

=== page
ISC: PROTECTED A
Despite funding increases in the 2023-2026 budget and the addition of 110 officers and
52 police support staff, the ratio of police officers to population has steadily declined. In
fact, the number of officers per 100,000 Calgarians is approximately 15% lower now that
it was a decade ago. Since 2019, CPS staffing has also grown at a 40% lower rate than
the rest of the City of Calgary Administration.
In anticipation of the upcoming budget, the Commission’s 2025 Community Perceptions
Survey asked Calgarians directly about their appetite for increased police funding:
• 57% thought that crime and social disorder are increasing in Calgary
• 44% believed current police funding is not enough (compared to 33% saying it is
the right amount, 8% saying it is too much, and 15% being not sure)
• 61% supported increased police funding in the 2027-2030 budget (with improved
staffing being the top priority)
• 45% were willing to pay higher taxes to better fund policing (compared to 25%
being unwilling and 30% being neutral)
• 66% preferred police funding be improved through a change in priorities for
existing municipal and police programs rather than a tax increase
CPS employees were also surveyed by the Commission in 2025, with concerning results:
• Only 11% of employees believe the CPS is adequately staffed
• Only 36% of police officers and 39% of police support staff said they expect to
still be with the CPS in five years
Finally, the number of CPS employees who are on leave or who require a medical
accommodation is close to one in every five. While there are a variety of reasons for this
high number, increased workplace stress and overtime is a significant contributor.
All these factors have informed the Commission’s position that the current CPS baseline
budget is wholly inadequate to provide effective policing moving forward in Calgary.
Significant growth is required in the next budget cycle to provide required service levels.
Proposed Budget Outcomes
The proposed 2027-2030 police business plan and budget is built on three priorities:
• Advancing Policing: Improving how the CPS investigates and disrupts crime,
including the adoption of modern technologies, tools and supports.
ii
ISC: UNRESTRICTED 2027–2030 Budget: Investing for the future 227

=== page
ISC: PROTECTED A
• Proudly Serving: Restoring frontline capacity, better supporting member
wellness and promoting strong governance or stewardship of police resources.
• Building Relationships: Upholding partnerships, advancing community-based
initiatives related to policing, and promoting collaborative policing approaches.
This budget provides a growth of 309 police officers and 214.5 police support staff,
along with critical upgrades to infrastructure and the tools and technology needed to
modernize policing in Calgary.
Of the 309 new police officer positions, 275 are required simply to ensure Calgarians
have the same number of officers per 100,000 residents as was originally intended when
the 2023-2026 budget was approved. This is what would maintain current service levels
with realistic workloads. However, the Commission does not believe this level of
resourcing would allow the CPS to provide adequate and effective policing into 2030
due to increased demands on policing generally and the trends we now see in Calgary.
Due to recruiting and training constraints, 309 is the most officers the CPS believes they
can add over the next four years. Police support staff are needed to both take over non-
policing functions currently being done by officers and to provide needed expertise that
enables the work of officers. These are tradespeople, analysts, recruiting and human
resource professionals, and similar functions needed to get as many officers as possible
doing the right work with the right equipment, training and supports.
Investments in new technologies, including artificial intelligence supports, online
reporting, drone technology, and cybercrime investigation tools, are also needed to
ensure officers are properly equipped and able to respond efficiently and effectively to
public safety issues. Additionally, investments are needed on the capital side in the CPS
vehicle fleet, information technology and communication infrastructure, as well as to
address facility maintenance that has been deferred for too long.
Return on Investment
The Commission knows that the 2027-2030 proposed police budget is substantial,
however, it is the result of underinvestment in policing over multiple past budget cycles.
Previous Commissions have worked hard to be good corporate citizens and keep police
budget increases as low as possible. But the CPS cannot continue to deliver the service
level expected by Calgarians with a baseline budget that has slowly eroded policing
capacity and employee wellness over the years.
iii
ISC: UNRESTRICTED 2027–2030 Budget: Investing for the future 228

=== page
ISC: PROTECTED A
The Commission and CPS have been prudent in the development of the 2027-2030
budget, ensuring that we are only requesting what we know we can spend. While this
budget technically includes growth, it is really only going to restore service levels to
what Calgarians had in the recent past.
With this budget (if both baseline and growth are approved), Calgarians will see:
1. Increased proactive policing, allowing officers to better seek out and prevent
social disorder, monitor prolific offenders, and prevent crime.
2. A needed reduction in emergency response times.
3. A maintenance or reduction in Calgary’s crime severity index value.
4. An increase in the percentage of Calgarians who feel safe, due to increased police
visibility and increased capacity to address crime and social disorder.
5. Improved police employee wellness.
6. Transformational change through the use of new technologies, like artificial
intelligence, drones as first responders, automatic licence plate readers, and
modern investigative tools.
7. Continued collaboration and cooperation with community partners to help
address the complex social needs in our community.
A Note on Capital Spending
Questions have been asked by some members of Council about the historically low
capital spend rate of the CPS. Two significant capital projects have largely been
responsible for this: a new district office in Belvedere and the new indoor firearms range.
The new district office funding is from a greenfield off-site developer levy and so must
be carried over year after year until a police station is built in that area. The City has yet
to even procure land for this new building, so the funding ($32.5 million) has appeared
on the CPS’ capital budget as unspent funding since 2021. The procurement process for
the indoor firearms range has also taken longer than expected, causing an additional
large unspent carryover amount to appear in the budget for the past couple of years.
CONCLUSION
The police budget has not kept up to population growth, which has significantly eroded
the CPS’ policing capacity and employee wellness over the past two budget cycles. The
Commission does not believe maintaining the CPS’ base budget will provide adequate
and effective policing into 2030, as required by the Police Act. We therefore respectfully
request that both the proposed baseline and growth budgets be prioritized by Council.
iv
