FROM THE CALGARY POLICE COMMISSION
FURTHER INFORMATION ON PROPOSED 2027-2030 POLICE BUDGET REQUEST
DATE: SEPTEMBER 25, 2026
PURPOSE: ☒ FOR INFORMATION ☐ OTHER:
APPROVED BY: AMTUL SIDDIQUI, COMMISSION CHAIR
REASON FOR THIS MEMORANDUM
Following the in-camera meeting with Council on July 28, 2026, this memorandum contains
additional information to help respond to the questions that were raised about the
proposed 2027-2030 police budget. An overview of the police budget request that the
Commission plans to provide to the public to support transparency is also attached.
DISCUSSION
As was outlined in a July 13, 2026, memorandum to Council, the 2027-2030 police business
plan and budget is a forward-looking budget that centres on providing more patrol officers
to the frontline and ensuring they have the tools, infrastructure and support to do their jobs
more efficiently and effectively.
It is also a catch up budget. The number of police officers per 100,000 Calgarians is
approximately 15% lower now than it was a decade ago. Since 2019, police staffing has also
grown at a 40% lower rate than the rest of the City of Calgary Administration. The impacts
of this are now showing through noticeably reduced service levels, decreased employee
retention, and more employees on medical leave and accommodation.
How the Budget was Developed
The typical process for developing the police budget starts with Council setting its overall
strategic priorities and a funding envelope for the entire municipality. The Commission and
Calgary Police Service (the Service) then work in consultation with City Administration to
develop a proposed budget for Council’s review and approval.
This year, the Commission followed a similar process to Council. The various units of the
Service submitted every budget request and the Commission and Service leadership then
worked together to cut items out of the budget that did not clearly support the
Commission’s priorities of improving frontline capacity, modernizing the tools available to
officers, and strengthening the community partnerships that provide a measurable return
for the police service.
1/7
ISC: UNRESTRICTED 2027–2030 Budget: Investing for the future 230

=== page
ISC: PROTECTED A
In total, $58 million of operating growth requests were not approved. These included
approximately 300 new FTEs, including positions like additional mounted patrol officers,
district front counter constables, specialized investigators (e.g., homicide and sex crimes
detectives), maintenance tradespeople, crime prevention community educators, forensic
accountants, communications staff, and administrative staff.
In addition to our annual strategic planning session, the Commission has spent
approximately 60-90 minutes of every monthly regular meeting since September 2025
providing strategic direction and approvals as part of the Service’s budget development
process to ensure we present Council with a prudent and necessary growth request.
Minimum Police Funding
Section 27(1) of Alberta’s Police Act requires municipal councils to maintain an “adequate
and effective” police service under the supervision of a police commission. The Alberta
Provincial Policing Standards define this term further by stating that, “[a] police service will
be deemed adequate and effective if the legislative requirements and policing standards are
met.” The standards further add that indicators of adequacy and effectiveness can include,
“legal requirements, compliance with standards, efficiency (e.g. cost/benefit per unit of
service) and timeliness.”
Council asked the Commission to provide both a baseline and growth request number as
part of the budgeting process. The Commission’s position is that maintaining current
baseline funding (even adjusted each year for inflation) is not an option as the Service is
already showing signs of not being able to provide adequate and effective policing.
While cracks are forming across the Service, here are some examples of what has led to the
Commission’s position that existing 2026 resourcing is not adequate:
• The Alberta Provincial Policing Standards require that frontline officers engage in a
variety of activities, including crime prevention, community engagement, traffic
enforcement, investigations, and preventative patrolling. Currently, over 80% of
frontline officers’ time is spent just responding to calls, rather than on these.
• Frontline teams are regularly using overtime and callout to maintain a minimum 60%
staffing level target for each shift. Accommodations, medical leaves, and employee
retention challenges are all contributing to this issue and overtime is not a cost-
effective or sustainable strategy to ensure sufficient staffing each shift.
• The Alberta Provincial Policing Standards require that police-controlled property be
maintained in a state of operational readiness. Deferred maintenance has put critical
2/7
ISC: UNRESTRICTED 2027–2030 Budget: Investing for the future 231

=== page
ISC: PROTECTED A
infrastructure at risk by not replacing HVAC units, roofs, electrical systems and
vehicles at the end of their lifecycles. Currently, there are police facilities that require
buckets in the hallways when it rains because of leaky roofs, and patrol teams are
regularly short vehicles because they are out of service for repairs.
• When urgent call volumes outstrip frontline capacity, the Service goes into
differential response. This means officers from across the city must be pulled from
their core duties and deployed elsewhere to handle emergency calls (similar to an
EMS “Code Red”). During this period, police may stop responding to non-emergency
calls altogether. The Service has doubled its differential response incidents from 10 in
2024 to 21 in 2025. This year, differential responses are on track to surpass 2025.
• Alberta’s Access to Information Act requires access to information requests from the
public to be fulfilled within 30 days, unless exceptional circumstances warrant an
extension. The Service is currently only completing 10.7% of these requests within
the legislated 30-day response deadline. While staffing in this area has been
increased this year, it is still indicative of civilian resourcing challenges.
As stated in our July 13 memorandum, our Commission believes that a return to the 2023
ratio of police officers per 100,000 Calgarians (requiring 275 new officers) would be the
minimum required to ensure adequate policing into the future. An additional 191 civilian
technical experts and support staff are also needed to ensure officers have the supports
they need to do their jobs. Significant portions of the capital budget are maintenance and
replacement costs to ensure the reliability of critical infrastructure after key maintenance has
been deferred over multiple budget cycles.
Additional Service Levels
The Alberta Provincial Policing Standards and Alberta Policing Oversight Standards both
allow for municipalities to provide a level of policing over and above the ”adequate and
effective” minimum, provided additional services are equitably provided to the whole
community and delivered efficiently.
The Commission’s annual community surveys and community engagement has shown over
and over that Calgarians expect additional policing services like School Resource Officers,
Diversity Resource Teams, and teams that support interventions in the lives of youth and
other people in crisis. It is this public input that is driving a budget request of a total 309 net
new officers, rather than just the 275 adequacy minimum.
The additional services provided by the police must be determined collaboratively by
Council and the Commission. Under the Police Act, Council ultimately decides how much
3/7
ISC: UNRESTRICTED 2027–2030 Budget: Investing for the future 232

=== page
ISC: PROTECTED A
Calgarians will pay for policing overall, but it is the Commission who decides through its
budget allocation what services above the adequacy requirements that funding will be used
to provide.
Civilian Technical Experts and Support Staff
The proposed 2027-2030 police budget includes both police officers and 214.5 net new
civilian FTEs. The vast majority of these positions support database management (entering
reports/warrants, searching records for officers, etc.), evidence disclosure, connecting
people in crisis to social services, IT maintenance and transformation (such as artificial
intelligence adoption), and crime analysis to connect trends and identify suspects. These
positions provide a direct benefit to frontline policing by providing tools to improve
efficiency and by completing tasks officers would otherwise have to do.
Around 15% of the new positions will support employee recruiting and training, employee
retention, and returning employees to work after a medical leave or accommodation. These
are needed to both help address the current number of officers on leave and
accommodation, and to hire and train the new officers being requested.
Around 9% are corporate supports, such as accountants, lawyers, payroll staff, business
strategists and communications staff. Another 9% are tradespeople and other asset
management professionals to ensure police infrastructure is adequately maintained.
Calgary Police Commission Budget
Questions were asked about the Calgary Police Commission budget. To protect the
Commission’s independence, it has an independent secretariat to support the board with its
duties. A small portion of the overall police budget is allocated to its operation.
The budget for the Commission’s operations has been unchanged for the last two budget
cycles at $1.39 million. This has supported 4.6 FTEs, an office lease, Commissioner
honorariums, a small community engagement event, staff and Commissioner training, an
annual community and employee survey, the Service’s external financial audit, and any other
external consultants (including legal counsel).
Over the past few years, the Commission has been trying to enhance its governance
practices while also absorbing inflation costs. At the beginning of 2025, the board decided
to transfer the Service’s internal audit function to the Commission staff team to transition to
a model like the City Auditor’s office. An independent governance and policy analyst was
also added to the team. Over the next budget cycle, the Commission would like to hire
4/7
ISC: UNRESTRICTED 2027–2030 Budget: Investing for the future 233

=== page
ISC: PROTECTED A
three additional internal auditors, bringing us in line with other policing organizations, and
one financial analyst to support our budget oversight.
In total, staffing growth, increased honorarium costs, and increased funding for outside
consultants and public engagement bring the proposed 2027-2030 budget to $3.19 million
per year (of which $1.3 million is net growth). The increased budget aligns with other major
cities and addresses several police governance challenges recently identified by the
province’s judicial review of the Edmonton Police Commission.
Outcomes of 2027-2030 Proposed Police Budget
The Commission has approved 10 key performance measures for the Service, the first three
of which will be reported quarterly to Council:
1. Proactive Policing Time: By 2030, proactive policing time will have increased by
14%. This means each frontline officer, on average, will have an additional hour and a
half each shift to proactively patrol, work with the community on crime prevention,
conduct traffic stops, enforce court conditions of people released on bail, monitor
prolific offenders, and proactively find and address disorder. Without a significant
increase to proactive policing time, Calgarians will experience the same level of
police visibility, crime prevention, and responsiveness as now.
2. Weighted Clearance Rate: Calgary has an above average case clearance rate
compared to other major Canadian cities, despite having a significantly lower-than-
average officer to population ratio. Investments in new technologies, civilian
investigative supports, and officer capacity will ensure the weighted case clearance
rate remains strong and even improves despite lower-than-average staffing levels.
Without these investments, the increasing complexity of crime and advances in
criminals’ use of technology is expected to erode the Service’s ability to solve crimes
over the next four years, reducing the weighted case clearance rate.
3. Emergency Response Time: Another benefit of increased proactive policing time is
that more units are available at any given time to respond to emergencies. The
Service’s average emergency response time target used to be 7 minutes, but
response times have slowly been worsening since 2022 and now sit above 13
minutes on average. Staffing growth will allow the police to consistently get to
emergencies within 12 minutes or less. New technologies like drone as a first
responder also support quicker response times by getting eyes on an incident in
progress sooner so that tactical decisions can be made and offenders can be located
before officers on the ground arrive. Without significant growth in frontline staffing,
response times are projected to continue getting worse as Calgary grows.
5/7
ISC: UNRESTRICTED 2027–2030 Budget: Investing for the future 234

=== page
ISC: PROTECTED A
4. Crime Severity Index: Increased proactive capacity and investigative technologies
are expected to further reduce Calgary’s overall crime severity index, which measures
both the frequency and seriousness of crime.
5. Community Perception of Safety: More police visibility and proactiveness is aiming
to increase the number of respondents who characterize Calgary as safe in annual
community surveys from 75% to over 80%.
6. Social Disorder Rate: Proactive work to address social disorder and enhance
community partnerships are expected to reduce the number of calls reporting social
disorder below the current three year average.
7. Traffic Safety: The exact metric is still being refined, but the Service and
Commission are likely to use a city-wide reduction in average speed as a measure of
traffic enforcement effectiveness.
8. Employee Engagement Index: Improved staffing will improve employee
engagement and retention, with the aim of increasing employees who report high or
moderate engagement from 59% to 65%.
9. Partnership Evaluation: A framework is under development to measure the
effectiveness of police partnerships with other agencies in the community.
10. Budget and Business Plan Performance: The Service is expected to fully spend
their budget (with the exception of any reserve contingency) and achieve at least
85% of their annual business plan deliverables.
CONCLUSION
Our Commission hopes the above information is helpful and addresses the questions that
were not clearly answered at the July 28, 2026, Council meeting. We have also included a
more detailed breakdown of the growth request as an appendix to this memo to increase
your insight into the police budget.
We are grateful for our strong working relationship with Council and look forward to
discussing the police budget with you further as we approach November.

move operations from reactive to proactive, helping The City keep pace with growth and better protect Calgarians from
future emergencies.

131 Police Vehicles
Department Business Unit
Calgary Police Services Calgary Police Services
Investment Description:
The Calgary Police Services (CPS) vehicle fleet enables patrol operations, investigative work and the work of specialized
units. Policing industry standards recommend replacing patrol vehicles at approximately 160,000 kilometers, with distinct
lifecycle thresholds for other vehicle classes based on usage and operating conditions. Deferred replacement in recent years
has resulted in a significant portion of the vehicle fleet operating beyond these standards, increasing repair costs, and
operational and safety risks, while proactive planning and data-enabled fleet management supports the continuity of police
services across The City.
Funding will support ongoing lifecycle replacement of the fleet ensuring previous deferral replacement of vehicles based on
expected standards is caught up by the end of 2030. Investment will also ensure the purchase and outfitting of required
vehicles to support workforce growth over the four-year planning and budget cycle. Two vehicles are required for every five
additional full-time police officers.
This investment has been identified as Required.

132 Cyber Security Program
Department Business Unit
Law, Legislative Services, & Security Cyber Security
Investment Description:
The City's Cyber Security Program brings together key investments that strengthen the protection of City services,
technology systems, and essential operations. The program improves The City's ability to prevent, detect, respond to, and
recover from cyber incidents, while supporting effective risk management, governance, and accountability as cyber threats
continue to evolve.
This enterprise-wide investment helps reduce the likelihood and impact of cyber incidents that could disrupt City services,
increase recovery costs, or negatively affect public trust. Cyber incidents experienced by municipalities across North America
have shown that the financial and operational impacts of an incident can far exceed the cost of prevention and
preparedness.
Investing in cyber security helps protect essential services, reduces the risk of service disruption, and supports reliable
operations. It also helps The City avoid costly recovery efforts, legal and regulatory challenges, and other long-term impacts
that can result from a significant cyber incident.
This investment has been identified as Required.

136 Canada Task Force 2
Department Business Unit
Community Services Emergency Management & Community Safety
Investment Description:
Canada Task Force 2 (CAN‑TF2) is Alberta’s disaster response team based in Calgary and managed by the Calgary
Emergency Management Agency (CEMA). Under the current funding model, 75 per cent of this investment is funded via a
federal government grant, with the City funding the remaining 25 per cent. This enables CAN‑TF2 to maintain readiness to
respond to large-scale disasters. The team partners with city services, emergency responders, corporations, communities,
and non-profits to support disaster response and recovery in alignment with Alberta’s Emergency Management Act. This
funding supports ongoing development of all-hazards response capabilities for Calgary and neighbouring communities,
including wildfire support, severe weather, and other major events and emergencies. Investments in this cycle include urban
search and rescue equipment, tents, and computers to support preparedness activities and real-time deployments. The
City’s full contribution is required to maximize federal funding, strengthening Calgary’s climate, economic, and social
resilience.

143 Industrial Control Systems Security Enhancements
Department Business Unit
Operational Services GM - Operational Services
Investment Description:
Operational Services lacks a unified, risk‑based cybersecurity program to protect the City’s most critical industrial control
systems (ICS). Key security gaps—including outdated or unsupported assets, limited monitoring, unmanaged remote access,
incident response gaps, and poor knowledge transfer—expose the City to significant operational, legal, and reputational
risk. As ICS environments become more interconnected, they face escalating cyber threats such as ransomware, data
breaches, and system outages. ICS risk mitigation remains siloed, fragmented, and reactive, resulting in inefficient
resourcing, lagging risk management, limited detection and response capability, and incomplete system visibility. To reduce
the likelihood and impact of disruptions, the City must invest in a comprehensive ICS Security Program aligned with the
Corporate ICS Security Standard. This investment would standardize and centralize ICS security across Operational Services
and other operators, strengthening governance and protection through a centralized ICS network while reducing costs and
disruptions.

153 Encampment Fire Protection – Bridge Infrastructure
Department Business Unit
Infrastructure Services Public Spaces Delivery
Investment Description:

bridge assets and preserves network operations.

154 Mobility Safety & Speed Management Improvements Program
Department Business Unit
Operational Services Mobility
Investment Description:
This program combines targeted speed management retrofits and physical safety modifications across collector corridors,
high-collision locations, and school zones to execute the Council-approved Calgary Safer Mobility Plan. Historical street
designs frequently conflict with operating targets, and posted signage alone cannot alter driver behaviour or protect
vulnerable users. By re-engineering the built environment, this program deploys physical interventions, including curb
extensions, raised crosswalks and medians, mid-street pedestrian safety islands, speed humps, and tightened curb radii.
Consolidating collector retrofits with broader mobility improvements resolves inconsistent speed environments, delivers
operational delivery efficiencies, and reduces severe injuries and fatalities across all Calgary communities.

ISC: UNRESTRICTED 2027–2030 Budget: Investing for the future 335

=== page
Primary Corporate Operating Risk: Community Safety risk
How will this investment manage or mitigate the Primary Corporate Operating Risk?
Operating historical roadway designs across collector corridors, high-collision locations, and school zones results in speeds
that exceed safe thresholds, increasing crash severity and exposure for vulnerable road users. This program deploys
physical, self-enforcing traffic calming and geometric layout changes, including tightened curb radii, narrowed lane widths,
and pedestrian refuges, to naturally regulate driver speeds and shorten crossing distances. Work is prioritized using
historical collision data, pedestrian activity, and school proximity. Modifications are coordinated with Calgary Fire and
Calgary Transit to preserve critical emergency and transit routes while aligning with scheduled pavement rehabilitation to
avoid construction rework.
Risk(s) of Not Proceeding (Approving) This Capital Spending Request
Deferring this investment maintains existing roadway configurations on collector corridors and key network locations,
limiting progress toward Council-approved safety benchmarks established in the Calgary Safer Mobility Plan. Response to
requests related to speeding, safer crosswalks, and school improvements will be limited, resulting in slower deployment of
safety improvements for vulnerable road users.
Risk(s) of Proceeding (Approving) This Capital Spending Request
At the proposed level of funding, this program delivers engineered traffic calming, speed management retrofits, and
roadway modifications across approximately 13 kilometres of prioritized collector corridors and high-collision locations over
the 4-year cycle. In-scope corridors experience annual collisions, injuries, and fatalities involving vulnerable road users,
generating societal costs and recurring municipal operational expenditures. Delivering physical modifications (such as
pedestrian refuges, raised medians, speed humps, curb extensions, and tightened curb radii) requires proactive stakeholder
engagement to manage localized community feedback regarding geometric alterations, curb shifts, and curbside parking
impacts. Capital will be directed to highest-incident locations and school zones rather than treating all eligible corridors
concurrently, non-prioritized segments must continue operating under existing roadway layouts in the interim. While
advancing this program achieves collision reductions and moderates operational costs, proceeding under the proposed
level of funding results in a delivery outcome that requires managing public expectations, careful corridor sequencing, and
close coordination with local civil contractor market capacity.

Risk(s) of Proceeding (Approving) This Capital Spending Request
Only the highest-priority investments were included in this request, creating a risk that accelerated growth or service
demands could outpace facility expansion. Future investment and collaboration across business units will be required to
support long-term objectives.

161 Emergency Operations Centre Lifecycle and Upgrades
Department Business Unit
Community Services Emergency Management & Community Safety
Investment Description:
The existing space at the Emergency Operations Centre (EOC) is increasingly challenged in supporting the needs of a
growing city and the increasing demands associated with major events, emergencies, and disasters. Over the last three
years, the EOC has been activated an average of 5 times per year. This investment will fund a feasibility assessment and
planning activities required to define future EOC expansion requirements, refine cost estimates, and inform subsequent
phases of capital investment.
Funding will also address priority maintenance and targeted upgrades to the current Calgary Emergency Management
Agency (CEMA) workspaces, including the backup EOC facilities. These improvements will enhance operational readiness
and ensure emergency management personnel can effectively coordinate responses to increasingly frequent and severe
incidents, including extreme weather and wildfires, while longer-term expansion plans are developed and implemented.

162 Supporting Transit Riders Through Longer Transfer Windows
Budget proposal rationale: Explicit Direction from Council
Department: Operational Services Business unit: Calgary Transit
Budget proposal description
This investment allows customers to travel farther and complete more complex trips for a single fare by extending the
transit transfer window from 90 minutes to 120 minutes. The extended window supports customers making longer
one-way journeys as well as round trip travel within a single fare, improving flexibility and convenience across the
network. This change responds to Council direction and enhances the overall customer experience by making transit
more affordable and practical for everyday travel. The additional investment offsets the expected revenue loss from
customers not buying a second fare in the 120-minute window. This budget item responds to Council direction arising
from a Notice of Motion (EC2026-0042, C2026-0285).
Proposed funding amount
2027 2028 2029 2030
One-time ($M) - - - -
Ongoing ($M) 2.0 - - -
FTEs* - - - -
*Number of Full Time Equivalents associated with this budget proposal
Performance metric: % Customer satisfaction with value for money of transit fares
Benefits of budget proposal
Extending the transfer window provides better value for money for 0.5% of Calgary Transit trips (by no longer requiring
a second ticket to be purchased between 90 and 120 minutes). While this will improve perceptions of value for some
users, it is a small segment of customers and therefore will have very small or negligible impact on our overall
satisfaction measures.

will miss opportunities to create a more livable and thriving city.

173 Ready to operate Green Line investment
Budget proposal rationale: Implicit Direction from Council
Department: Operational Services Business unit: Calgary Transit
Budget proposal description
Supports planning and staffing readiness to operate the Green Line, scheduled to open in 2031, with some phases
opening earlier. Transit must recruit, train and certify operations, engineering, and maintenance staff in advance of
opening day. This will enable safe and reliable operation of the new system, which includes new low-floor vehicles,
signaling, and maintenance facilities. While permanent operating funding is being accumulated, it will not be available
until 2032. One-time funding is required to bridge this gap and ensure staff, systems, and emergency partners are ready
for launch. Without it, the system risks being physically complete but not ready to operate on day one.

to ensure that the system can be operated reliably and safely on opening day. This budget proposal will allow safe and
reliable Green Line operations by ensuring that staff are properly trained and prepared for passenger service.

176 New Levy Funded Traffic Signals / Development Infrastructure -
Arterial Development
Department Business Unit
Operational Services Mobility
Investment Description:
This program funds the annual construction of new traffic signals supported through Off-Site Levies to integrate expanding
communities into the municipal transportation network. Driven by community growth, new intersections, and construction
cost inflation, installing these signals to manage complex arterial access is required under the municipal Traffic Bylaw.
Leveraging developer-funded levies prevents a backlog of uncontrolled intersections, reduces collision risks, and ensures
safe connectivity in new subdivisions.
This investment has been identified as Required.

This program funds the construction of new traffic signals required to integrate expanding communities. Installing these
signals ensures mobility infrastructure keeps pace with land-use intensification and prevents new intersection construction

At the proposed funding level, this program delivers the annual construction of new traffic signals supported through Off-
Site Levies to integrate expanding communities into the municipal network. New intersection construction, community
growth, and contractor cost adjustments require installing traffic signals as prescribed in the municipal Traffic Bylaw and
Off-Site Levies bylaws. The primary operational consideration is ensuring controlled crossing points keep pace with
developing roadway networks, subject to market conditions and timing dependencies on private sector development
schedules. Developers require coordinated signalized traffic controls to support opening new roadways. Capital funding
directly dictates installation capacity, with each $500,000 adjustment correlating to approximately one signal installation.
Funding this investment in line with the 2027-2030 need leverages developer-funded off-site levies to fulfill infrastructure
commitments, optimize regional traffic flow, lower greenhouse gas emissions from idling, and ensure safe multi-modal
environments for new subdivisions.

phased improvements to the MAX Green, including terminal expansions and streetscape improvements. These upgrades
enhance comfort and convenience for passengers while strengthening the Primary Transit Network. Off-Site Levy (OSL) is
assumed to be part of the project's capital cost estimate. If OSL is partially or not provided, the project can still proceed but
less improvement would be implemented.
Risk(s) of Not Proceeding (Approving) This Capital Spending Request
Not investing prevents infrastructure enhancements along the MAX Green BRT corridor, constraining Primary Transit
Network performance and limiting service quality to key destinations, including downtown Calgary.
Risk(s) of Proceeding (Approving) This Capital Spending Request
At the recommended funding level, full buildout of the RouteAhead Primary Transit Network MAX Green BRT corridor will
not be realized, requiring project scope to be prioritized among transit priority lanes, intersection measures, BRT stations,
streetscape and terminal facilities, alongside complex urban infrastructure delivery and traffic management during
construction.

Risk(s) of Not Proceeding (Approving) This Capital Spending Request

Risk(s) of Proceeding (Approving) This Capital Spending Request

identified pedestrian safety hazards. Current network conditions sit at 67 per cent good, 31 per cent fair, and 2 per cent
poor for sidewalks, and 79 per cent good, 20 per cent fair, and 0.5 per cent poor for curb and gutter, compared to approved
Level of Service targets of 54 per cent good, 46 per cent fair, and 0 per cent poor for sidewalks with a 72 per cent hazard
reduction. Curb and gutter rehabilitation must precede roadway paving, as unsynchronized delivery requires excavating
recently resurfaced roadways, shortening pavement lifecycles and increasing lifecycle costs. Full funding stabilizes sidewalks
at 54 per cent good, 45 per cent fair, and 1 per cent poor by 2030 while clearing 29 per cent of the safety hazard backlog,
with curb and gutter tracking at 81 per cent good, 18 per cent fair, and 1 per cent poor. Constraining funding compounds
reactive repair costs, expands liability exposure, and delays coordinated pavement resurfacing across established
communities.

among Calgarians to reduce their impact on land consumption and the potential for flooding.
ISC: UNRESTRICTED 2027–2030 Budget: Investing for the future 429

=== page
Primary Corporate Operating Risk: Growth Risk
How will this investment manage or mitigate the Primary Corporate Operating Risk?
Continuous build-out of the citywide Pathway Network. The primary risk is that persistent infrastructure gaps between
schools and parks restrict equitable transportation options for non-drivers. Aiming to add 20 kilometres annually, this
program targets the closure of connectivity gaps, resulting in better utilization of existing and funded infrastructure. This
investment provides safe, reliable travel options for the one-third of Calgarians who do not drive, connecting communities
through a unified network.
Risk(s) of Not Proceeding (Approving) This Capital Spending Request
Deferring this investment limits the planned expansion of dedicated, separated active mobility infrastructure, requiring users
of non-vehicular modes to continue utilizing existing roadway shoulders and shared street cross-sections along unbuilt
corridors. Without dedicated capital to close identified network gaps, connections between established neighbourhoods,
local schools, transit hubs, and employment areas will remain reliant on existing street configurations. This sequencing
extends the delivery timeline for citywide active transportation targets, maintaining current physical boundaries across
multi-community corridors and pacing network connectivity across future capital budget cycles.
Risk(s) of Proceeding (Approving) This Capital Spending Request
Delivering the pathway program under the proposed funding level paces active transportation network expansion,
constructing approximately 7.5 km of pathway over four years to connect key community destinations, employment hubs,
and transit stations. Operating within this funding level prioritizes the highest-impact links identified in the 10-year
implementation plan. However, this level of funding requires deferring lower-priority segments and candidate investments
with completed designs. This creates potential delivery inefficiencies, as deferred designed packages may require updating
in future budget cycles, while limiting near-term opportunities to synchronize construction with adjacent capital works. In
the interim, deferred links will be actively managed through targeted operational retrofits and temporary safety measures to
maintain safe connectivity across network gaps.

Primary Corporate Operating Risk: Asset Risk
How will this investment manage or mitigate the Primary Corporate Operating Risk?
This investment addresses structural deterioration, localized slope instability, and sudden corridor closures across the active
network. Completing scheduled structural rehabilitations of aging asphalt pathways, granular trails, and pedestrian bridges
restores assets in poor condition, extends structural service life, and ensures safe, continuous active mobility year-round.
Risk(s) of Not Proceeding (Approving) This Capital Spending Request
Reduces the City's ability to achieve corporate targets for active transportation and public safety, while increasing the
likelihood of structural asset failures and unscheduled closures of primary pedestrian corridors.
Risk(s) of Proceeding (Approving) This Capital Spending Request
Deteriorating pathway and bridge assets remain in poor condition longer, increasing the risk of localized structural failures,
unexpected corridor closures, and significantly higher future rehabilitation costs. Program delivery involves coordination and
cost challenges across a distributed, diverse asset base, requiring detailed management of slope stability and environmental
erosion issues. Under the proposed funding allocation, the program enables the full replacement of approximately 4,300
metres of poor and failing asphalt annually, the rehabilitation of approximately 800 metres of granular trails in natural parks,
and limited replacement of failing trail structures. However, this level of capital investment leaves an estimated 27 km of
unreplaced pathways over the 2027 to 2030 budget cycle. This deferred lifecycle maintenance accelerates network decline,
potentially reducing the share of pathways rated in fair or better condition from 92 per cent to as low as 75 per cent.
Residents will experience localized disruptions, detours, and compromised access to reliable active transportation
connections. Additional funding based on 2027 to 2030 capital needs replaces an additional 10,300 metres of asphalt and
1,800 metres of granular trails annually, maintaining 90 per cent to 95 per cent of the overall asset inventory in fair or better
condition. Fully funding this investment ensures bridge structures reach their 100-year design life, protects natural park
systems, and delivers safe, continuous active mobility across the municipal network.

233 Citywide Growth Strategy – Established Area Public Realm
Enhancements
Department Business Unit
Infrastructure Services Public Spaces Delivery
Investment Description:
This strategic investment program funds targeted public realm and active mobility improvements within established
communities experiencing redevelopment and population growth. Accounting for 43 percent of all new housing in the city
in 2025, established areas require concurrent upgrades to public spaces, pedestrian infrastructure, and community facilities
to support densification while maintaining livability. Guided by the Municipal Development Plan (MDP) and Local Area
Plans, the program funds both major capital corridor investments and localized, community-led enhancements. Sustaining
this funding is required to incentivize private investment, help fulfill the 50/50 growth split policy, and ensure that legacy
infrastructure supports the pressures of modern urban intensification.

Primary Corporate Operating Risk: Growth Risk
How will this investment manage or mitigate the Primary Corporate Operating Risk?
This program funds enhancements in established communities experiencing intense redevelopment. The primary risk is that
legacy infrastructure cannot support the pressures of modern urban intensification, compromising livability. Guided by the
Municipal Development Plan, the program funds community amenity improvements, including parks, open spaces, and
corridor investments and localized upgrades. This is required to incentivize private investment, fulfill growth split policies,
and ensure neighborhoods remain functional and attractive to new residents and businesses as they densify.
Risk(s) of Not Proceeding (Approving) This Capital Spending Request
Would lead to declining public space quality and reduced livability. Active projects would require alternative funding to
continue and may otherwise face cancellation, introducing reputational risk and reducing public trust. Growth within
established areas would be less effectively prioritized for investment, reducing the success of the 50/50 growth split policy.
Risk(s) of Proceeding (Approving) This Capital Spending Request
Proceeding under the proposed funding level adjusts the investment pipeline, deferring capital delivery timelines by four to
six years or until additional funding is identified. Consequently, existing infrastructure will continue to manage increasing
service demands relative to local population growth, moderating the pace of achieving corporate targets for the 50/50
growth split between established and greenfield communities.

235 Habitat Restoration
Department Business Unit
Infrastructure Services Public Spaces Delivery
Investment Description:
The Habitat Restoration Annual Investment Program delivers targeted restoration activities that protect and strengthen
natural assets. Investing in natural infrastructure today helps address issues early, reducing the need for more costly repairs
and emergency interventions in the future. This proactive approach also helps safeguard pathways, roads and utilities,
supports safe and accessible park spaces and protects the long-term value of public assets.
Natural assets are an important part of Calgary's infrastructure network. They provide the air we breathe and the water we
drink, protect built infrastructure, enhance community wellbeing and contribute to the City's resilience. Calgary's natural
areas are valued at approximately $6.9 billion and face increasing pressures from erosion, heavy use, invasive species and
urban development.

ISC: UNRESTRICTED 2027–2030 Budget: Investing for the future 497

=== page
Primary Corporate Operating Risk: Asset Risk
How will this investment manage or mitigate the Primary Corporate Operating Risk?
This investment reduces Asset Risk by protecting Calgary's natural infrastructure and improving the health and resilience of
natural areas. Maintaining these assets helps prevent environmental degradation, supports the continued delivery of
ecosystem services, and reduces the likelihood of more costly repairs or restoration in the future. As a result, the City's
natural assets can continue to provide long-term value to Calgarians.
Risk(s) of Not Proceeding (Approving) This Capital Spending Request
Without this investment, the condition of Calgary's natural infrastructure will continue to decline, leading to higher future
restoration and maintenance costs. Projects that are currently lower priority may become more urgent and costly to address
over time, resulting in further loss of habitat quality, ecosystem services, and community benefits. As natural assets degrade,
they become less effective at providing benefits such as erosion control, water management, and access to nature, while
requiring increased operating and maintenance resources. Calgary's natural infrastructure has an estimated replacement
value of $6.9 billion and provides approximately $2.5 billion in annual ecosystem services, making proactive investment
critical to protecting these long-term community and financial benefits.
Risk(s) of Proceeding (Approving) This Capital Spending Request
At this funding level, pressures on natural infrastructure (e.g., invasive species, unsustainable human use and urban
development) will continue and exceed the rate of restoration. Restoration is dynamic, highly variable and a long-term
process (projects are generally 7–10 years in duration and restoration itself takes decades). As such, the on-the-ground
results of these projects may not be observable for many years. The overall condition of our natural assets will decline and
not be able to achieve the council priorities of Community Livability and Well-being or Reliable and Sustainable
Infrastructure. The return on investment for natural infrastructure projects is estimated at 6-10:1.
The program advances key targets in Connect: Calgary's Parks Plan. With this level of funding, the targets of restoring 1,000
hectares of land by 2035 or improving the overall condition of Calgary's natural areas will not be met. The benefits of
maintaining natural assets in good condition will also decrease, including The City’s ability to reduce future costs, manage
risks, and ensure these spaces continue to provide environmental, social, and infrastructure benefits for Calgarians.

237 Park Infrastructure Lifecycle
Department Business Unit
Operational Services Parks & Open Spaces
Investment Description:
This program keeps Calgary’s parks safe, usable, and in good condition, while delivering on the Connect: Calgary's Parks
Plan and Council priorities. It funds ongoing repairs and replacements so park assets stay at a “Fair” condition or better.
The program supports playground lifecycling, repairs and upgrades to sports fields and courts, culturally significant sites,
signage, paved areas, lighting, fences, and other park features across the city. The program also supports irrigation and
drainage systems so that water is managed effectively and parks are kept healthy.
Some important park features—like those in Devonian Gardens, event furnishings, and cemetery assets—also need
investment as they are key to how parks look, feel, and function.
The current funding level supports the Council-approved playground lifecycling (IP2026-0034 Playground Sites Level of
Service, Option 4), in which no permanent playground removals will be required.
Right now, 18 per cent of parks assets are in Poor and Very Poor condition. Without funding, Poor or Very Poor assets will
need to be removed and not replaced, while some Fair assets may decline in the near future. Investing now keeps parks
safe, accessible, and enjoyable, while avoiding higher future costs and service gaps.

Risk(s) of Not Proceeding (Approving) This Capital Spending Request
Without this investment, aging athletic park components will continue to deteriorate, increasing the risk of asset failures,
closures, safety concerns and service disruptions. More extensive rehabilitation or replacement may be required as asset
condition declines, increasing future lifecycle costs and reducing the reliability and availability of athletic park amenities.
Risk(s) of Proceeding (Approving) This Capital Spending Request
At the recommended funding level, available funding will be focused on a limited number of priority athletic park
rehabilitation projects. This will address condition and service risks at selected locations, while aging components at other
locations will remain outstanding. Over time, continued deterioration may reduce playing quality and hours of operation,
increase the risk of closures and safety concerns, and result in higher lifecycle costs. Reduced field availability may also place
additional pressure on the remaining athletic park inventory. Shifting funding outside of 2027 will impact athletic parks that
are highly used by the community. Delaying the replacement of the components at these parks will affect structural integrity
and increase the life safety risk, it will also impact the hours of operation and the primary function of the field. Limiting the
number of hours and uses of the fields will lead to a decrease in revenue, inability to meet the needs of the community and
increase dissatisfaction in City services.

Investment Description:
The Parks and Playgrounds Amenities Program (PAPA) invests in neighborhood and sub-neighborhood parks where

Neighbourhood and sub-neighbourhood parks are among the most frequently used public assets in Calgary and play a
critical role in providing accessible recreation, gathering spaces and informal play close to home. The program supports
timely upgrades not addressed through lifecycle or major capital programs, ensuring local parks remain safe, inclusive, and

241 Calgary Public Library Investment Program
Department Business Unit
Civic Partners Civic Partners
Investment Description:
The Calgary Public Library serves all of Calgary with 52 per cent of Calgarians holding active memberships. The service
provision standard for community libraries is 0.3 square feet per capita. As Calgary continues to grow, library services must
grow to ensure all residents continue to have access to the resources, services, and connections that build strong
communities. This investment will fund the construction and redevelopment of two libraries to increase capacity as Calgary
grows. It is anticipated to add approximately 25,000 square feet of library space and improve access in areas experiencing
service pressure. The Calgary Public Library Investment Program invests in land purchase, design, and construction of
libraries in new communities and revitalization of libraries in existing communities to maintain service targets and adapt to
evolving visitor needs.

246 Urban Forestry - MDP Target
Department Business Unit
Operational Services Parks & Open Spaces
Investment Description:
This program seeks to grow Calgary's urban forest to meet Municipal Development Plan (MDP) tree canopy targets, and
supports Connect: Calgary's Parks Plan (Connect) objectives, through planting new trees across the city. It will contribute to
expanding the urban forest towards the objective of a 16 per cent tree canopy by 2060 by planting 360,000 trees from 2027
to 2028. Federal funding supports roughly half of the planting up until 2028 (IP2026-0356, Advancing Tree Equity through
the 2 Billion Trees Program), but further investment is required to plant more trees in 2029 and 2030 to keep on track with
urban canopy targets.
A healthy, resilient, growing urban forest improves the quality of life of Calgarians. Funding sustainable urban tree canopy
growth provides many long-term benefits such as shade during extreme heat events, clean air and water, and vibrant, green
spaces. Without investment, it is expected that a 1 to 2 per cent increase per decade in the urban tree canopy cannot be
achieved. Ongoing capital funding is needed to make progress towards the 16 per cent by 2060 MDP target and Connect's
target of planting 1.3 million trees by 2035.

The Connect Plan directs the protection and enhancement of the tree canopy, in alignment with the 16 per cent canopy
target by 2060 in the MDP. To meet the tree canopy and equity target, we need to plant more trees than we remove every
year and improve conditions for tree success in low canopy neighbourhoods.
Communities with a lower tree equity can face higher health risks. Tree canopy cover reduces the risks associated with
extreme weather events, such as long periods of heat. Trees also help to lower heating and cooling costs and can increase
property values. This level of funding is below the amount required to improve tree equity in 2029 and 2030.
Risk(s) of Not Proceeding (Approving) This Capital Spending Request
Without this investment, Calgary’s tree canopy would grow more slowly, reducing progress toward the MDP target of 16 per
cent canopy by 2060 and limiting opportunities to improve tree equity in lower-canopy communities. The City would also
lose approximately $11.3 million in federal funding if it does not meet the contribution agreement requirement for $12
million in matching tree-planting investment from all program sources in 2027 and 2028.
Risk(s) of Proceeding (Approving) This Capital Spending Request
At the recommended funding level, approximately half of the planned tree planting can be completed during 2027–2030.
Net-new planting would occur in 2027 and 2028, but no net-new trees would be funded in 2029 or 2030, and community
planting initiatives, including Branching Out, would not be funded in those years. This interruption slows progress toward
the 16 percent canopy target and limits tree-equity improvements. Trees added through the program also create ongoing
requirements for establishment, maintenance, risk management and inventory that must be supported through operating
resources.
ISC: UNRESTRICTED 2027–2030 Budget: Investing for the future 520

=== page
Primary Corporate Operating Risk: Capital Funding Risk
How will this investment manage or mitigate the Primary Corporate Operating Risk?
Investing in cemetery development now helps keep costs down over time. Capital funding addresses aging facilities and
adds needed space before problems become urgent. This reduces the need for costly emergency repairs and service
disruptions. Planning ahead allows work to be done in stages, protects existing assets, and helps manage budgets
responsibly, avoiding higher future costs. By investing now, we can ensure that cemetery services remain reliable, respectful,
and accessible for today's families and future generations.
Risk(s) of Not Proceeding (Approving) This Capital Spending Request
Calgary’s growing population requires updated cemetery amenities to meet community expectations. Cemetery
maintenance standards are provincially legislated. Underinvestment may result in accessibility challenges, higher
maintenance costs and declining assets, which may lead to increased regulatory and public scrutiny if cemeteries are not
maintained to expected standards. Without investment, families will face fewer end-of-life service options, more service
delays, pressure on existing cemetery capacity will increase, and opportunities to generate revenue that supports ongoing
maintenance and perpetual care will be constrained.
Risk(s) of Proceeding (Approving) This Capital Spending Request
At the proposed level of funding, small improvements to cemeteries can be made such as improved signage, site furniture,
regional pathways and a boardwalk. The current funding level does not support needed irrigation system projects, utility
upgrades, development of additional lands, or a multiuse gathering centre, requested by communities. Without major
improvements, there may be reduced revenues, which impacts the perpetual care fund and long-term sustainability.
Building strategic cemetery infrastructure commits The City to upfront costs and coordination, but meets community needs,
adds capacity in a planned way, and supports reliable, respectful essential services over the long term. Partial funding would
further limit the City's ability to expand capacity and complete supporting infrastructure improvements, reducing future
revenue opportunities and increasing long-term service and financial risks.

direction to target a “Good” service level for public-tree removal and replacement.

the existing backlog and maintaining ongoing lifecycle replacements reduces reliance on reactive removals and enables
operating resources to focus on inspection, pruning and proactive tree care. Replacement planting also establishes the next

needs will continue to emerge as trees age or decline, so priorities may change based on condition and safety assessments.
Replacement trees also require ongoing establishment and maintenance, creating an operating requirement that must be
sustained for lifecycle investment to achieve its intended long-term benefits.

260 Mobility Network Planning Studies

Investment Description:
This program funds quadrant and local planning area network studies to comprehensively evaluate Calgary's transportation

interchanges, flyovers, and arterial widenings, ensuring infrastructure delivery aligns with community growth.

City business units.

equipment would reduce operational flexibility, increase maintenance and operating costs, and create greater risk of service
delays, reduced reliability, and unmet Council-approved service commitments. Any reduction in funding for Vehicle &
Equipment Growth would require corresponding reductions to frontline service capital programs and associated service
levels.

growth, infrastructure expansion, and increasing service demands. The impact would extend beyond Fleet & Inventory.

maintain, inspect, and support new infrastructure and services. Without corresponding fleet growth, those investments may
be unable to achieve their planned service outcomes, reducing the value and effectiveness of the broader capital program.
More plainly – you can hire the people and build the infrastructure, but if the vehicles and equipment are not there, the
service capacity still doesn’t exist.

ability of crews to perform work simultaneously across a growing city.

under or over-utilized depending on our client business units’ capital program funding. In addition, added fleet may strain
maintenance, storage, vendor and operator capacity, impacting service continuity.

Benefits:
This investment helps ensure Calgarians have access to the services and community amenities they rely on as the city grows.

This includes investment in fire stations, recreation centres, libraries, parks amenities, public washrooms, and arts and

Primary Corporate Operating Risk: Operational Risk
How will this investment manage or mitigate the Primary Corporate Operating Risk?
This investment reduces operational and asset risks by renewing facilities with identified condition, functional or accessibility
needs and adding capacity where existing infrastructure does not meet service requirements. Renovations and
replacements reduce reliance on aging facilities, while new and expanded facilities address identified service and growth
needs. A portfolio approach also allows The City to prioritize investment based on asset condition, service need and project
readiness.
Risk(s) of Not Proceeding (Approving) This Capital Spending Request
Without this investment, planned renewal, replacement and expansion of community and emergency-service facilities would
not proceed. Aging community and emergency service facilities will continue to deteriorate, resulting in higher maintenance
costs, increased operating expenses, and a greater risk of service disruptions and facility closures. Facilities awaiting
modernization, expansion, or replacement may fail to meet accessibility standards, capacity requirements, or community
expectations, reducing service quality and reliability. These issues will worsen as population growth and demographic shifts
place additional demands on existing spaces. Service enhancements and growth initiatives under GamePLAN may be
delayed or halted due to inadequate infrastructure. Delaying investment in new fire stations and the replacement of aging
downtown stations will increase response times and compromise firefighter and public safety by overextending crews and
relying on outdated facilities. Delaying investment will also raise future capital costs as facilities age and rehabilitation needs
grow. Ultimately, this will reduce access to community services, increase service inequities across Calgary, and limit
opportunities to develop integrated, multi-service facilities that improve efficiency and customer experience.
Risk(s) of Proceeding (Approving) This Capital Spending Request
At the recommended level of funding, the portfolio will advance two major renovations, four facility replacements and four
new builds. Many facility expansions, modernizations, and replacements will be delayed or limited to planning and design,
rather than construction. This will postpone community benefits, service capacity improvements, and asset upgrades, while
increasing reliance on aging infrastructure, maintenance demands, and safety risks. Delaying lower-priority projects will
require additional future funding, and the overall costs will increase due to inflation and market escalation. While the
portfolio approach allows flexibility to advance the most ready projects, many community infrastructure needs will be
shifted to future budget cycles, further extending timelines for service and capacity improvements.

Primary Corporate Operating Risk: Operational Risk
How will this investment manage or mitigate the Primary Corporate Operating Risk?
The Downtown Amenity Fund establishes an adaptive funding approach across the four-year budget cycle to support rapid
residential growth in the core. This flexible model provides the tactical agility required to deploy capital toward park
upgrades, recreational amenities, and safety enhancements. By delivering improvements as needs arise, the fund prevents
civic infrastructure from lagging behind urban densification, maintaining a safe, vibrant, and fully functional downtown for
residents and visitors.
Risk(s) of Not Proceeding (Approving) This Capital Spending Request

upgrades to parks, open spaces, and pedestrian corridors would be sequenced over a longer timeframe, requiring mature
core infrastructure to absorb ongoing densification without concurrent capacity adjustments. This approach limits near-term
delivery of targeted safety and placemaking enhancements, increasing the need to manage community expectations
regarding the pace of downtown public realm investments.
Risk(s) of Proceeding (Approving) This Capital Spending Request
Approval of the Downtown Amenity Fund establishes an adaptive approach but requires ongoing prioritization among
competing core improvement opportunities within a finite funding envelope. Because demand is expected to exceed
available funding, trade-offs will be required between scale, timing, geographic distribution, and overall community impact
across six priority allocation areas: Recreation & Community Amenities; Emerging Needs & Event-Based Opportunities;
Activation, Partnerships & Potential Matching Funds; Parks, Open Space & Placemaking; Safety, Lighting & CPTED
Enhancements; and Public Realm & Streetscape Improvements. The fund's flexible nature requires transparent, responsive
decision-making to align project selection with emerging core priorities and manage evolving public expectations. Future
funded works may also introduce operating and maintenance impacts that must be evaluated as scopes are confirmed,
balancing tactical agility with long-term financial sustainability to safeguard inner-city quality of life amid intense residential
densification.

create ongoing holding costs, while site investigations may identify conditions that affect suitability or future development
costs. Clear acquisition criteria and due diligence are required to manage these risks.

Grounded in the principle of “For Indigenous, By Indigenous,” the Maa’too’maa’taapii Aoko’iyii’piaya program addresses

demonstrating the number of projects that are ready to advance with funding. This capital investment will provide
additional funding to build capacity within the community and support the delivery of culturally safe, non-market homes for
Indigenous Calgarians.

sustainability objectives.

=== page
Primary Corporate Operating Risk: Asset Risk
How will this investment manage or mitigate the Primary Corporate Operating Risk?
Uncertain project scopes and preliminary technical assumptions lead to project cost escalation and a shortage of shovel-
ready candidates for intergovernmental funding programs. This program establishes a dedicated planning framework to
define technical requirements and risk profiles early, creating a structured pipeline of coordinated, cost-effective transit
projects.
Risk(s) of Not Proceeding (Approving) This Capital Spending Request
Without this investment, there would be delayed or poorly informed future capital decisions, increasing project risk and cost
escalation. The risk of not proceeding is to lose the opportunity to secure matching funds through the Strong Transit Fund
and other external funding oppportunities. If this happens, the City will have to pay 100% of the funds, rather than cost
sharing with other levels of goverments.
Risk(s) of Proceeding (Approving) This Capital Spending Request
At the recommended funding level, this program would advance feasibility and functional planning work for priority transit
projects identified in RouteAhead, the 2020-2050 Fleet Facilities and Infrastructure Plan, as prioritized in the 10-Year Plans.
At this funding level, this program leaves approximately $10.5 million of planned functional planning and feasibility work
unfunded, requiring some studies to be deferred, and project development level of work reduced. This funding gap will
delay planning progress, limit the evaluation of potential corridor and alignment options, and increase the likelihood of
future cost and schedule impacts as additional work is advanced in subsequent funding cycles. If the funding level is further
reduced, this will limit the funding opportunities from the federal and provincial governments due to projects not being
ready. Full funding maintains a robust pipeline of shovel-ready transit investments.

288 Civic Census Program
Budget proposal rationale: Explicit Direction from Council
Department: Planning & Development Business unit: City & Regional Planning
Services
Budget proposal description
This proposal requests operating funding to reinstate Calgary’s Civic Census program. The census provides a consistent,
citywide source of discrete geographical population, dwelling and household data not available from other sources.
Census data is foundational to strategic growth, service planning, infrastructure investment, funding allocation and
performance measurement. Reinstating the census will restore a core planning and accountability function, improve
measurement of outcomes and indicators, and support evidence based decision making for Council, Administration,
service areas and external interested parties (universities, school boards, hospitals, citizens, orders of government).

resources, assess infrastructure investment per resident and track progress against Council approved outcomes. The
census supports consistent performance measurement across service areas, improves transparency and accountability,
and reduces reliance on modeled or proxy data. Access to reliable population data strength‑ens business cases,
improves fiscal stewardship, and enables more informed policy and investment decisions that reflect actual conditions
on the ground.

292 Resourcing Prairie Economic Gateway Delivery
Budget proposal rationale: Explicit Direction from Council
Department: Chief Operating Office Business unit: Chief Operating Officer
Budget proposal description
This operating budget request invests in Calgary’s next chapter—creating the dedicated capacity to deliver Prairie
Economic Gateway as a city-shaping platform for trade, jobs, and long-term competitiveness. It keeps Calgary leading in
provincial and federal funding windows by aligning partners and governance, producing grant-quality submissions,
and driving disciplined project management that moves Council-approved direction from plans to delivery readiness. It
is a modest operating commitment that protects eligibility, sustains momentum, and positions Calgary to win
investment decisions—and deliver with confidence.
Proposed funding amount
2027 2028 2029 2030
One-time ($M) 4.2 - - -
Ongoing ($M) 3.3 1.2 - -
FTEs* 10 4 - -
*Number of Full Time Equivalents associated with this budget proposal
Performance metric: $ External capital funding per capita
Benefits of budget proposal
Gateway is a defining opportunity to position Calgary as the Prairie’s pre-eminent inland port—connecting local
innovation to global markets and strengthening resilient supply chains. It leverages an exceptional 9:1 private-to-public
investment ratio, helps unlock approximately $6B in private capital, and supports an estimated over 30,000 jobs, with
an immediate increase of $1B in additional goods moved annually. By shifting long-haul freight from roads to Class 1
rail, it reduces pressure on municipal infrastructure, improves road safety, and lowers emissions intensity. This
operating investment keeps Gateway credible, competitive, and ready to win—and deliver—when funding windows
open.

305 Recognize impact of changes to photo radar regulations
Budget proposal rationale: Responding to Provincial Government Changes
Department: Corporate Programs Business unit: Corporate Programs
Budget proposal description
As part of the 2026 budget adjustments, Calgary Police Service moved fine revenue to Corporate Programs to allow it to
make enforcement decisions without managing the revenue implications. The transfer also recognized a $28 million
shortfall, arising from changes to provincial photo radar regulations. For 2026, this shortfall was funded via the fiscal
stability reserve. While the proposal addresses this shortfall in 2028-2030, funding limitations in 2027 mean a temporary
“least-harm” approach will be required to redirect resources to cover the expected shortfall.
Proposed funding amount
2027 2028 2029 2030
One-time ($M) - - - -
Ongoing ($M) - 28.0 - -
FTEs* - - - -
*Number of Full Time Equivalents associated with this budget proposal
Strategic alignment
Primary Council strategic priority Primary community outcome Community indicator
Trusted & Collaborative Government The City sets balanced taxes and fees, Calgarians’ perception of value for tax
providing Calgarians with good-value dollars
for their money.
Corporate strategic pillar/desired state: Financial Sustainability Financial decisions are tied to strategy
and outcomes
Alignment to long-term plan: 2023-2026 Service Plans and Budgets
Risks
Primary risk that this proposal is managing/mitigating Primary risk rating
The Municipal Government Act requires municipal governments to adopt balanced High
annual operating budgets. Therefore, any significant, reasonably foreseeable decreases in
revenues must be accounted for. The risk of revenue shortfalls in 2025 and 2026 was
mitigated through the Fiscal Stability Reserve. With the understanding that provincial
photo radar regulations are expected to continue, it is prudent to treat this as an ongoing
concern rather than address it year by year. 2027 funding constraints mean that a “least-
harm” approach will need to be taken to address the shortfall; impacts cannot be assessed
until budget approval.

311 Enterprise Planning Module (The City's budgeting system)
replacement implementation and sustainment costs
Budget proposal rationale: Explicit Direction from Council
Department: Corporate Planning & Financial Business unit: Finance
Services
Budget proposal description
Finance currently has capital funding and has begun procurement for to replace Hyperion, The City's budgeting system
(EPM). This request moves the software licensing from capital to operating as well as provides implementation and
ongoing sustainment support.
Proposed funding amount
2027 2028 2029 2030
One-time ($M) 0.9 0.7 0.2 0.2
Ongoing ($M) - - - -
FTEs* 4 - - -
*Number of Full Time Equivalents associated with this budget proposal
Performance metric: # of days past month-end close for delivery of Executive Information Report (EIR) to CFO
Benefits of budget proposal
A permanent, centralized EPM sustainment team preserves and applies the knowledge embedded in the financial
model, including dimension structures, business rules, allocations, and calculation logic. Modern EPM platforms are
metadata driven so understanding how the model behaves is as critical as the data it contains. Without continuity,
report development slows as teams repeatedly rebuild structures that already exist. A permanent EPM team ensures
new reports reuse established structures, minimizes errors and enables Finance to focus on explaining why results
changed. This capability is essential to meeting growing expectations from ELT and Council for faster reporting and
timely insight.

319 Sustainable Building Resources for Industry and Developers
Budget proposal rationale: Risk-based considerations
Department: Planning & Development Business unit: Environmental Risk & Resilience
Services
Budget proposal description
This budget proposal includes education and resources co-developed and co-implemented with industry partners for
industry partners, to measure and track building performance data and pursue cost-effective high-performance
building measures that increase building durability, lower operating costs, and improve occupant affordability, health,
and safety. Includes enhancements to the Green Building Priority Stream Program through the inclusion of pre-
approved high-performance design plans to accelerate permit approvals, release of an online Calgary-specific
Sustainable Building Guidebook, and low-cost training sessions to upskill trades. This Program is unfunded in 2029 and
2030.

Benefits of budget proposal
This proposal supports more public and private building owners to track and measure their building performance
through BenchmarkYYC. This proposal helps these participants, as well as the broader industry, to improve energy
efficiency and energy performance in their buildings, resulting in overall energy use reduction and operational savings.
Funding is proposed for 2027 and 2028 only. Without funding in 2029 and 2030, service levels will decline and
performance metrics are expected to remain static after 2028.

321 Customer Service Modernization
Department Business Unit
Corporate Planning & Financial Services Assessment & Tax
Investment Description:
Assessment & Tax is currently operating with several unintegrated customer service systems. This creates internal
inefficiencies and service delivery gaps across our customer touchpoints. The recommended funding supports delivery of
the foundational Customer Relationship Management (CRM) for coordinated service delivery across all channels, and
improved oversight of customer inquiries and service outcomes. To align with the updated corporate funding level, MyTax
portal enhancement will be reduced and digital customer experience enhancements will be deferred. As a result, certain
self-service capabilities will not be implemented, resulting in ongoing digital service gaps for customers and continued
reliance on staff-assisted service.
This investment has been identified as Required.

=== page
Primary Corporate Operating Risk: Community Relations Risk
How will this investment manage or mitigate the Primary Corporate Operating Risk?
Modernizing and integrating our core customer service systems is urgent. To meet community expectations, Assessment &
Tax needs a single coordinated system to track, manage and respond to service requests across divisions and service teams.
The revised funding recommendation protects the core CRM integration and case management capabilities needed to
support that work. This is especially important because some MyTax enhancements have been deferred, limiting the
automation and advanced self-service functions that can be delivered. As a result, some customer interactions will continue
to require manual processing and staff support. Stronger tracking and coordinated response will help reduce service gaps,
improve accountability and maintain public trust.
Risk(s) of Not Proceeding (Approving) This Capital Spending Request
The project is already in implementation. If funding does not proceed, the time, effort and money already invested in
planning, configuration, testing and training would not deliver their intended value. Assessment & Tax would be left with an
incomplete rollout and continued reliance on fragmented inquiry channels, manual workarounds and duplicate processes.
This would limit visibility into customer requests, weaken ownership and accountability, extend response times, and create
fragmented handoffs across service tiers. It would also reduce reliable performance reporting and make it increasingly
harder to meet public expectations for accessible and responsive service.
Risk(s) of Proceeding (Approving) This Capital Spending Request
The recommended funding was reduced by 53% from the original scope, and 50% of the remaining 2027 funding was
postponed to 2028 and 2029. Extending delivery of customer modernization initiatives over a longer timeframe increases
schedule, cost, and implementation risk. Project costs may increase due to changing market conditions and resource
availability. Delays between development, testing, and deployment may result in additional rework, quality assurance effort,
and resource pressures. A longer implementation timeline may increase coordination requirements with related initiatives
and delay the realization of planned operational efficiencies, service improvements, and business benefits. Continued
reliance on existing processes and interim workarounds may also create ongoing operational, resourcing, and change
management challenges.

322 Tax System Modernization
Department Business Unit
Corporate Planning & Financial Services Assessment & Tax
Investment Description:
This investment replaces aging tax systems that support over $3.7B in annual revenue and are essential to delivering
legislated billing and collection services. These systems are reaching end of life, with increasing failure risk, limited flexibility,
and growing reliance on manual workarounds to maintain operations. Without replacement, there is a high risk of service
disruption, challenges meeting legislative requirements, and impacts to consistent revenue collection and customer service
delivery. The investment includes phased delivery from planning and procurement through implementation, testing, and
stabilization, ensuring continuity of operations while reducing risk throughout delivery. This modernization will strengthen
system reliability, improve operational efficiency, and enable digital service enhancements such as electronic notifications
and enhanced self-service, supporting accessible, reliable, and efficient services for Calgarians.
This investment has been identified as Required.

324 HR Software Learning Management System
Department Business Unit
People, Innovation & Collaboration Services Human Resources
Investment Description:
The City’s Learning Management System (LMS) is a core enterprise application used to administer, track, and report on
employee learning, including mandatory and legislated training, supporting compliance with health, safety, and regulatory
requirements. The current vendor is discontinuing support, creating significant operational and compliance risks if not
replaced.
Without a supported LMS, The City cannot reliably manage certifications and required training, exposing it to legal,
regulatory, and safety risks. It would also result in fragmented, duplicative solutions across business units, increasing costs
and raising data security, privacy, and governance concerns.
This investment will replace the LMS with a modern, secure, vendor-supported platform to ensure continuity of learning
services, maintain compliance, and protect corporate investments. The project is in implementation, with a vendor selected,
and this budget supports delivery in 2027.
This investment has been identified as Required.

325 Calgary City Net
Department Business Unit
People, Innovation & Collaboration Services Information Technology
Investment Description:
Calgary City Net is a high-speed data network backbone that provides network services/connectivity to support current and
future business needs of The City. Business Units are adopting technology to become more efficient and effective in their
operations and in the delivery of services. Technology adoption by business units enables access to real-time information
through greater use of remote sensors and mobile applications. Remote monitoring of conditions, remote control of
devices and services, and real time data capture in the field can assist in crisis management, community engagement, and
result in operational efficiencies.
Calgary City Net provides dedicated funding for the lifecycle, maintenance, modernization, and growth of the City’s core
network services. This includes enterprise Wi Fi, network security appliances, and the Calgary City Network backbone within
City facilities. This investment ensures this high-speed backbone continues to be sustainable, resilient, scalable, and secure
to support the delivery of essential services to the Corporation and to Calgarians.
This investment has been identified as Required.
